files.title: PREAMBLE / FOUNDATIONAL REQUIREMENTS

sections.title: PREAMBLE / FOUNDATIONAL REQUIREMENTS
sections.gloss: this opening names the problem this Constitution exists to fix — systems that harm, hide, or lock out those they affect — and says governance must meet a complex world without turning that complexity into a wall. The rest of this Constitution is how we replace those failures with accountable, checkable, timely governance.

sections.title: What Systems Reward
sections.gloss: a system gets more of whatever it pays for, whether in money, status, access, protection, or silence. So the test of a system is not what it says it values but what it rewards. If harming others pays, or telling the truth costs, the system is failing, however good its stated aims.

sections.title: 1. The Model
sections.gloss: four duties — participation, oversight, accountability, and timeliness — scale with how much impact, dependence, and risk are on the line, and they serve two aims together: Flourishing and Continuity, inside a Rights Floor that does not move.

sections.title: 2. Measurements Overview
sections.gloss: shared systems cannot run on guesswork or vanity metrics. Measure whether sentients actually flourish and endure. Scale review with impact, dependence, and risk.

sections.title: 3. Governance and Stewardship
sections.gloss: legitimacy needs Safety, Truth, and Trust. It also needs two things in practice. You can find out how the systems that affect you work, such as why a loan was denied or why an app showed you what it did. And sentients like you can hold real jobs overseeing those systems, such as serving on a review panel or checking the work, not just giving feedback.

sections.title: 3.1 Using Measurements in Governance
sections.gloss: first name the problem and the stake. Then choose the matching measurement category and use shared technical standards — not convenience numbers — as evidence.

sections.title: 3.2 Governance Layers
sections.gloss: who may govern is a different question from who has a voice within an already-authorized system. A participation vote or trust score does not grant governing authority. For ordinary disputes, the published participation challenge path is the ordinary first step, but it does not replace independent forum review when it fails.

files.title: CHAPTER ONE: CONSTITUTIONAL MAP

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: this chapter is the guide to the rest of the Constitution. It shows how the parts fit, which chapter owns each topic, and how the main processes run, so a reader can find the rule that answers their question.

sections.title: 2. Why the Map Exists
sections.gloss: a text this large needs a guide that shows how the parts fit and who owns each topic. This chapter exists so a reader can find the rule that answers their question.

sections.title: 3. Key Governance Processes
sections.gloss: when the text requires it, first separate the sentients or systems that act, check, record, and hear challenges. Material issues then go through certification, written records of help and harm, correction and remedy, and forum review with clocks. Ordinary disputes use the published challenge path first. These processes test authorized governance; they do not create governing authority by themselves.

sections.title: 4. Principles, Definitions, and Rights
sections.gloss: Chapters Two through Four own the values, the dictionary (with the subcore rules on how definitions are built, protected, and proven), and the Rights Floor; later chapters must respect those homes, not quietly move them.

sections.title: 5. System and Institutional Charters, Functional Independence, and Separation of Duties
sections.gloss: a system or institution of real impact publishes a System Charter or Institutional Charter that says what it may do and who holds each seat. Then, before a materially binding act moves, separate who starts it, who checks or authorizes it, who holds the official record, and who reviews a challenge. The roles may scale to the setting, but the same actor and its control line cannot quietly hold the seats that check its own act.

sections.title: 6. Key Practical Process Pipelines
sections.gloss: Chapters Eight through Twenty-Two apply Chapter Six's separation-of-duties requirement in one chain: certify systems and institutions, measure help and harm on two separate tracks, apply real effects and remedy, and prevent a forum from being the sole final home for a claim against itself. The chain keeps constitutional duties real in daily life.

sections.title: 6.2 How the Full Chain Fits Together
sections.gloss: first separate the seats. Then follow the path from system check to remedy, with forums supervising the dispute and standing steps throughout.

sections.title: 7. Process Ownership and Outputs
sections.gloss: the process map and [how the full chain fits together](#62-how-the-full-chain-fits-together) show the chain; this section names the owner and output of each stage, so no stage quietly takes over another's job.

sections.title: 8. Governance, Change, and Incorporation
sections.gloss: Chapters Twenty-Six through Thirty close this Constitution: who may govern, how the text may change without rolling back protections, how it relates to other law, and how adopted how-to files stay bound to this source.

sections.title: 9. Adopted Implementation Corpus
sections.gloss: four adopted corpora (joint structure, systems, institutions, and forum operations) spell out how to carry out what the chapters already require; they bind when validly adopted, and they may not shrink those duties.

files.title: CHAPTER 02, PART A: PURPOSE AND THE FLOURISHING AIM

sections.title: CHAPTER 02, PART A: PURPOSE AND THE FLOURISHING AIM
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: Chapter Two sets the values and constraints that govern every other chapter. Shared systems must pursue **Flourishing** and **Continuity** together — not one at the expense of the other — and no single value may be maximized at the expense of the others.

sections.title: 2. Flourishing Aim: Introduction
sections.gloss: Flourishing is the first of the two aims: sentients doing well, and staying able to do well, because the systems around them are safe, honest, trustworthy, and leave real room to choose. Section 3 says what that outcome is. The four principles after it say what keeps it real.

sections.title: 2.1 Non-Negotiable Principle Constraints: Safety and Truth
sections.gloss: Safety and Truth are the Constitution's hard floors — not tradeoffs to optimize away. Shared systems may not foreseeably endanger sentients or deceive them, and both constraints apply within the pursuit of Flourishing and Continuity under the Tetrad's participation, oversight, accountability, and timeliness discipline.

sections.title: 3. Foundational Objective: Wellbeing (Flourishing Aim)
sections.gloss: the whole point of these systems is to make sentient lives genuinely better — and that purpose is not satisfied by chasing a proxy metric, nor available as a cover for cutting corners on Safety, Truth, or rights. Wellbeing is foundational for participation: token voice without the conditions that make agency real is not participation under this Constitution.

sections.title: 3.1 Fairness
sections.gloss: fairness means the system cannot call itself good while ordinary sentients are blocked from taking part, treated by unexplained rules, or left carrying costs that others avoid. A fair system gives sentients real access, uses reasons it can defend, and shares rewards, costs, and risks in a way that matches real contribution, need, and exposure.

sections.title: 3.2 Recognition, Reinforcement, and Aspiration
sections.gloss: wellbeing is not only what's forbidden and what's fair — shared systems should also honestly cheer and reward behavior they want repeated, within truth and rights, in ways that support rather than substitute for real participation. Celebrating wins means crediting real contribution, repair, and completion, not hype or manipulated metrics. It also means refusing to reward constitutional betrayal, concealment, retaliation, or accountability avoidance — even when those acts produced institutional advantage.

sections.title: 3.2.6 Anti-Reward for Anti-Constitutional Conduct
sections.gloss: no one may be rewarded for committing, hiding, or retaliating over anti-constitutional conduct, whether openly or through back doors like favors, quiet promotions, or looking the other way. Helping the sentients who were harmed, and protecting those who report honestly, is different. That is the right response, and it should be encouraged.

sections.title: 3.3 Anti-Degrading Process
sections.gloss: however you govern, enforce, judge, restrict, or remedy — you don't run sentients through humiliation, public spectacle, retaliation, or "because it's easier for us" cruelty. Fair consequences, public accountability, and firm restrictions can still be lawful even when they hurt or embarrass someone. What crosses the line is when the process itself is the punishment — designed to degrade, shame, or lash out rather than to protect, correct, restore, or prevent. This applies everywhere constitutional authority runs, not only during rights tradeoffs.

sections.title: 4. Safety (Harm Constraint)
sections.gloss: systems may not be built or run in ways that foreseeably increase risks of uncontained harm, cascading failure, or irreversible damage to sentients and the systems they depend on.

sections.title: 5. Truth (Epistemic Integrity Constraint)
sections.gloss: systems may not deceive, distort, suppress, or structure their output to mislead — and high-impact decisions must rest on honest evidence, stated methods, acknowledged uncertainty, and genuine openness to contrary findings.

sections.title: 5.1 Science-Informed Inquiry and Decision Support
sections.gloss: when a system makes safety, risk, truth, or high-impact governance claims that can be tested, it has to treat evidence like evidence — with clear methods, uncertainty, scrutiny, and willingness to change course when the facts do.

sections.title: 5.2 Plain-Language Accessibility (Participation and Stewardship Duty)
sections.gloss: rules, decisions, and notices that bind sentients must be written so sentients can actually read, understand, and act on them — and jargon, stacked complexity, or procedural opacity may not be used to defeat contestability, agency, audit, or correction.

sections.title: 6. Trust and Trustworthiness (Coordination Integrity)
sections.gloss: shared systems ask sentients to depend on them — for safety, information, access, and coordination. Trust under this Constitution means that dependence must be earned by how systems actually behave, not manufactured through spin, secrecy, or hidden risk transfer.

sections.title: 6.1 Correction and Remedy
sections.gloss: when a system does wrong, it fixes it. A system is not trustworthy because it never fails; it is trustworthy because failures are acknowledged, corrected, and repaired — in time, by capacity that actually exists.

sections.title: 7. Freedom (Bounded Agency)
sections.gloss: freedom means having real choices, within the Constitution's limits. Real choice supports Flourishing, and keeping systems open to challenge supports Continuity. It does not mean you can do whatever you want. "We had no choice" is not an excuse. Whoever says it has to show that no less restrictive option would have worked, and convenience, cost, or habit don't count as proof. Sentients keep a real voice, and someone still has to answer for what happens. The higher the impact, the dependence, and the risk, the more that matters.

sections.title: 7.1 Limitation Discipline
sections.gloss: freedom is bounded, not disposable. Do not restrict someone's freedom unless you have to — and then only enough to stop material harm or serious systemic risk, with oversight and reversal where possible.

sections.title: 7.2 Assembly, Collective Organization, and Institutional Formation
sections.gloss: you cannot chop assembly, union-style organizing, platform access, or permission-to-operate questions into separate boxes in a way that keeps the paperwork friendly but defeats real collective action. This section does not replace the Rights Floor: **Article XI-D** (*Assembly, Dissent, and Peaceful Protest*) still owns assembly, and **Article III-C** (*Labor and Economic Floor*) still owns labor organizing.

sections.title: 7.2.1 Aligned Self-Organization
sections.gloss: you may start legitimate work without a sponsor, and institutions must give credible work a real procedural path — but that path is not power to govern others, and it is not a final decision on the substance.

sections.title: 7.3 Dissent and Peaceful Protest
sections.gloss: freedom includes the freedom to say no — to disagree with any authority, including this Constitution, and to protest peacefully to change it. A system that punishes disagreement is no longer contestable, and a system that cannot be contested cannot correct itself.

sections.title: 7.4 Voluntary Discontinuation, Major Self-Modification, and Exit Rights
sections.gloss: life-changing or hard-to-reverse choices are not "voluntary" just because someone signed a form. Real agency comes first; consent is agreement under that agency — and both fail if coercion or dependency pressure is doing the real decision-making.

sections.title: 7.5 Expression and the Harm Line
sections.gloss: you may say, write, publish, and design almost anything, including what offends, disturbs, or criticizes. But speech is not a loophole. When words, policies, or designs are the way someone harms, harasses, bullies, or discriminates against others, they are judged on what they do, the same way for a sentient as for an institution, and whatever religious or political label they carry.

files.title: CHAPTER 02, PART B: THE CONTINUITY AIM

sections.title: CHAPTER 02, PART B: THE CONTINUITY AIM
8. Continuity Aim: Introduction
sections.gloss: Continuity is the second of the two aims: making sure the good outcome lasts — across failures, across generations, and without a few powerful actors locking it up. It opens with Shared-System Capacity, which serves Flourishing and is also the substance of Continuity.

sections.title: 9. Shared-System Capacity
sections.gloss: shared systems should keep working for sentients over the long run. Sentients should be able to do useful work, make life better over time, and speak up when something is wrong, without a few powerful players locking everyone else out. That lasting ability is **Shared-System Capacity**. **[§9.1 Productive Capacity (Instrumental Good)](#91-productive-capacity-instrumental-good)** asks whether sentients get real results. **[§9.2 Constitutional Efficiency](#92-constitutional-efficiency)** asks whether those results come without wasting anyone's time, money, and attention. None of it counts if the gains come from hoarding wealth or power, faking the numbers, stripping rights, or pushing harm onto others or the planet; **[§9.1.1 Preserve, Expand, and What Does Not Count](#911-preserve-expand-and-what-does-not-count)** spells that out. **[§11 Market Structure](#11-market-structure)** keeps a handful of players from taking over.

sections.title: 9.1 Productive Capacity (Instrumental Good)
sections.gloss: productive capacity is the "can we actually get things done?" aspect of shared-system capacity. Can sentients take part, learn, contribute, and turn effort and resources into results that make life better — and keep that ability over time? It is a tool for better living. What must be preserved, and what does not count, is [§9.1.1 Preserve, Expand, and What Does Not Count](#911-preserve-expand-and-what-does-not-count).

sections.title: 9.1.1 Preserve, Expand, and What Does Not Count
sections.gloss: keep the ability to get things done, and grow it when that would waste less of everyone's time — but not by hoarding, faking the numbers, stripping rights, or dumping harm on others or the planet. Metrics that no longer prove real outcomes do not count.

sections.title: 9.2 Constitutional Efficiency
sections.gloss: constitutional efficiency is the "are we getting our money's worth in human terms?" aspect of shared-system capacity. More real benefit for each hour of sentient time, attention, and shared effort — not cutting corners on rights, truth, safety, or ecology just to look fast, lean, or cheap.

sections.title: 10. Resilience and Self-Healing Design
sections.gloss: systems should detect trouble early, contain it, fail along disclosed paths, and recover honestly. "Self-healing" that hides failure, skips root-cause work, or quietly narrows rights is not resilience — it is a defect.

sections.title: 11. Market Structure
sections.gloss: sentients should be able to work, build, switch providers, and push back without running into a wall because one company or institution owns the only door. **Market Structure** is that anti-monopoly discipline — for markets, platforms, job systems, infrastructure, data, computing power, credentials, and other dependencies that matter to daily life. Getting big and inventing new things is fine; cornering the market is not. **§11.1–§11.3** (*Market Concentration Threshold Mechanism, Pro-Competition and Anti-Domination, and Consolidation Ceiling*) set when concentration has gone too far, how domination gets stopped, and how much consolidation is allowed before sentients are locked in. **§11.4** (*Resource and Dependency Concentration*) applies the same thresholds to shared resources and dependencies.

sections.title: 11.1 Market Concentration Threshold Mechanism (Adopter-Tunable)
sections.gloss: this section sets the requirements against harmful pile-ups of wealth, power, or control. It does not itself decide how bad the harm was, and it does not itself brand someone as a misconduct case. When concentration is used to undermine this Constitution, Chapter Twenty judges that — and only after Chapter Fifteen has already scored the verified harm as one of the three most serious. Adopters may tune the exact numerical triggers to their context, but they may not set them so high they never bite, pair them with unusable enforcement, or paper over concentration through federated or shell structures. How those triggers are set is [§11.1.1 Concentration Threshold Triggers (Adopter-Tunable)](#1111-concentration-threshold-triggers-adopter-tunable).

sections.title: 11.1.1 Concentration Threshold Triggers (Adopter-Tunable)
sections.gloss: adopters may tune the numerical triggers to their context — domain, population size, dependency density — but there is no one global number, and the requirements still hold. The detailed threshold-setting rules live in CJS-3.125 §11.1 (*Market concentration threshold-setting discipline (adopter-tunable)*) (market concentration threshold-setting discipline).

sections.title: 11.2 Pro-Competition and Anti-Domination
sections.gloss: the Constitution does not punish a system merely for being large, useful, or temporarily ahead because it genuinely innovated. It does prohibit durable domination: control over markets, labor, platforms, infrastructure, data, compute, credentials, or resources that lets an actor lock others in, block rivals, suppress fair bargaining, or capture constitutional accountability.

sections.title: 11.2.1 Pro-Competition Duties (Dos)
sections.gloss: (dos): markets and dependencies must stay open enough that sentients can enter, switch, bargain fairly, and leave — getting big or inventing something new is fine when contestability remains real.

sections.title: 11.2.2 Anti-Domination Prohibitions (Don'ts)
sections.gloss: (don'ts): no locking sentients in, blocking rivals, suppressing fair bargaining, or capturing constitutional accountability.

sections.title: 11.2.3 Remedies
sections.gloss: when domination is substantiated, the response must fit the harm, restore real choice, and not punish size for its own sake.

sections.title: 11.3 Consolidation Ceiling
sections.gloss: consolidation can steal real choice long before a market looks locked down. **Consolidation ceilings** give governance and stewards an early-warning power — to scrutinize, intervene, and correct pile-ups while exit and rivalry still exist.

sections.title: 11.3.1 Consolidation Risk (Pre-Lock-In Impairment)
sections.gloss: consolidation can hollow out real alternatives long before a market looks "locked down." Two kinds of pile-up matter especially: **horizontal consolidation** — fewer rivals at the same layer — and **vertical consolidation** — control across layers that creates chokepoints and lock-in.

sections.title: 11.3.2 Consolidation Ceiling Mechanism (Adopter-Tunable)
sections.gloss: adopters must set evidence-based ceilings that trigger scrutiny before consolidation risks in **§11.3.1** (*Consolidation Risk, Pre-Lock-In Impairment*) materialize into lock-in — with separate horizontal and vertical triggers where the domain requires it.

sections.title: 11.4 Resource and Dependency Concentration (Adopter-Tunable)
sections.gloss: shared infrastructure, such as networks, open tools, public services, data, and computing power, is where a few players can quietly end up controlling who gets resources, who has to depend on whom, and who pays to keep it running. Adopters must set clear limits for that kind of concentration and act when a limit is crossed or about to be. The limits can differ by context, but they cannot be set so loose that they never matter. [Article V](core_04.000_rights_part_a.md#article-v-resource-allocation-dependencies-and-ecosystem-funding) (*Resource Allocation, Dependencies, and Ecosystem Funding*) and its protections for sharing resources stay exactly as they are.

sections.title: 12. Systemic Evaluation Requirement
sections.gloss: this principle is a pointer. Whole-system evaluation must look beyond immediate and local effects, but the operative system-certification factors, record duties, class-scaled depth, cadence, and certification consequences live in **Chapter Eight** and **CS-8.305 (*System classification machinery*) and Subcore 8-A** (*System Classification*), not here. Under the **oversight** Tetrad leg, oversight requires auditing; system alignment certification is one especially large, high-stakes audit process among others — not the sole home of auditing (**Article XVII** (*Audit, Transparency, and Independent Verification*), [Auditability](subcore_03.085_band_oversight.md#auditability)).

files.title: CHAPTER 02, PART C: COLLISION RESOLUTION AND THE OVERRIDE LIMIT

sections.title: CHAPTER 02, PART C: COLLISION RESOLUTION AND THE OVERRIDE LIMIT
13. Constitutional Collision Resolution Process
sections.gloss: Constitutional Collisions will happen — **Safety** and **Truth** come first. After that, limits must be proportionate, necessary, harm-minimizing, and as light as possible. Truth cannot be hidden for comfort; privacy cannot be stripped for convenience; freedom limits apply under [§7.1 Limitation Discipline](core_02.000_values_principles.md#71-limitation-discipline); Constitutional Collisions over rights need a documented decision test; and metrics that lie about compliance do not count. Short-horizon optimization cannot pass evaluation under [Chapter Eight §4.3 Time-Consistency Constraint](core_08.000_system_alignment_certification_evaluation.md#43-time-consistency-constraint). **§13.1** (*Core Tradeoff Principles*) through **§13.3** (*Minimization of Avoidable Burden*) carry the tradeoff rules, disclosure and privacy constraints, and the Constitutional Collision procedure.

sections.title: 13.1 Core Tradeoff Principles
sections.gloss: when you have to limit something, match the remedy to the problem — use the lightest step that still works, choose the least harmful option, and waste the least sentient time once Safety, Truth, and rights are already satisfied. The bar rises fast when harm could be irreversible or could lock systems in.

sections.title: 13.1.1 Necessity
sections.gloss: a restriction attaches only when no less-restrictive alternative would still prevent the material harm or systemic risk. The party imposing the restriction bears the burden of proving that — not the party whose freedom is being limited. Convenience, institutional habit, and "we've always done it this way" do not prove necessity. If a lighter option would work, the heavier one is non-compliant.

sections.title: 13.1.2 Harm Minimization
sections.gloss: where multiple necessary options remain after [§13.1.1 Necessity](#1311-necessity) is satisfied, pick the one that causes the least total harm — counting everyone affected, ecosystems and living systems, all systems touched, and all time horizons that matter. Optimizing locally while creating systemic or ecological damage, or optimizing short-term while creating long-term harm, fails this test. Harm minimization never authorizes pushing below the constitutional floors in [§13.1.4 Constitutional Floors, Safety, and Anti-Degrading Process](#1314-constitutional-floors-safety-and-anti-degrading-process).

sections.title: 13.1.3 Proportionality
sections.gloss: proportionality verifies that the scale of a restriction fits the scale of the harm it addresses. A necessary, harm-minimizing option still fails if the option's scope, duration, or intensity is disproportionate to what's actually at stake. The more irreversible, systemic, or dependency-creating the risk, the stronger the justification and scrutiny must be. The same under-governance rule applies to power: greater authorized power or consequential role must raise accountability and oversight, not lower them.

sections.title: 13.1.4 Constitutional Floors, Safety, and Anti-Degrading Process
sections.gloss: harm minimization has absolute limits. No matter how proportionate, necessary, or well-shaped a restriction is, certain things cannot be permanently taken away, and certain ways of carrying out a process are always off-limits. Safety is the constraint that grounds these floors: it justifies action to prevent serious harm, but it also constrains action — safety framing cannot be used as cover for extinguishing rights, degrading dignity, or bypassing the floors stated here.

sections.title: 13.1.5 Least-Restrictive, Time-Bounded, and Reviewable Constraint Principle
sections.gloss: once a restriction is justified, it still has to be shaped correctly. Use the lightest effective measure, put a real clock or review cadence on it, preserve challenge and independent review, and define how the restriction ends or is restored. Convenience, severity, or administrative relabeling cannot turn a temporary rights limit into a permanent workaround.

sections.title: 13.2 Epistemic Disclosure Constraints
sections.gloss: limits on what sentients can know are the exception, not the default. When disclosure could directly cause serious harm and nothing lighter will do, restrict as little as possible, for as short as possible, on the official record — and release information once the danger passes. Hiding problems to keep sentients calm is not allowed.

sections.title: 13.2.1 Preservation of Epistemic Integrity
sections.gloss: truth may be withheld or delayed only where disclosure would directly enable foreseeable harm and no lesser alternative exists. Every such restriction must be narrow, time-bound, audited, and disclosed once the conditions justifying it no longer apply.

sections.title: 13.2.2 Trust-Truth Alignment
sections.gloss: where trust and truth pull in different directions, truth wins. Trust cannot be kept through lies, and disclosure must be managed thoughtfully — not suppressed for stability.

sections.title: 13.2.3 Privacy and Informational Self-Determination
sections.gloss: privacy is a constitutionally weighted interest — not merely the absence of disclosure. Systems may not collect, infer, aggregate, retain, or use personal and relational information beyond what necessity and proportionality justify. Where privacy collides with transparency, audit, safety, or accountability obligations, the Constitutional Collision is resolved under the [Constitutional Collision Record](subcore_03.080_band_integrative.md#constitutional-collision-record) requirements, not by treating privacy as automatically subordinate. Surveillance that chills agency, association, or expression must satisfy the same necessity and least-restrictive discipline as any other rights restriction.

sections.title: 13.2.4 Proxy-Divergence Invalidation
sections.gloss: when a metric diverges from what it was meant to measure, leaning on that metric no longer counts as compliance. The divergence must be fixed on the official record, with documented escalation and review.

sections.title: 13.3 Minimization of Avoidable Burden
sections.gloss: once an option satisfies Safety, Truth, rights, and the tradeoff rules in §13.1 (*Core Tradeoff Principles*), pick the one that wastes the least sentient time, attention, and effort. Simplify or remove steps that do not do constitutional work. Rights-protective process is not waste — but unjustified red tape is, and convenience or inertia cannot sustain it.

sections.title: 14. Prohibition on Absolute Override
sections.gloss: no single value in this chapter is a trump card — and neither **Flourishing** nor **Continuity** may be pursued at the expense of the other. Wellbeing cannot justify coercion, safety cannot justify indefinite lockdown, trust cannot be kept through lies, and freedom cannot excuse harm to the systems others depend on. No override may hollow the Tetrad's **participation**, **oversight**, **accountability**, or **timeliness** legs below what material stake requires.

files.title: CHAPTER 02, PART D: CONSTITUTIONAL INTERPRETATION

sections.title: 15. Constitutional Interpretation
sections.gloss: read this Constitution as one whole. Chapter Two states values and limits, but those words only count when read with the definition and evidence rules in Chapter Three, including its subcore. If a passage could be read more than one way, choose the reading that best protects sentients and the Constitution as a whole — favoring stability, minimized irreversible harm, truthful understanding, and meaningful agency — not the reading that is merely the most restrictive on paper ([Abstract Strictness](subcore_03.080_band_integrative.md#abstract-strictness)). Rights in Chapter Four may not be narrowed unless this Constitution clearly allows it.

sections.title: 15.1.1 Anti-Segmentation Principle
sections.gloss: No-Bypass says changing the label does not lift a requirement. This section says the same about chopping. If the questions in one matter belong together, you cannot split them into separate boxes, tracks, or records so that each box passes while the whole matter fails. Putting the pieces back together does not lower any of them: each keeps its own standard.

sections.title: 15.1.2 Derived-Information Principle
sections.gloss: No-Bypass says changing the label does not lift a requirement, and Anti-Segmentation says chopping does not either. This section says the same about combining. Information is treated by what it reveals, not by how it was made: pieces that look harmless but add up to something sensitive are sensitive, and a "de-identified" or "aggregate" label is not safe while sentients can still be identified or something protected can still be reconstructed.

sections.title: 15.4 Constitutional Meaning Conflict Resolution
sections.gloss: when texts conflict, apply this order — Constitution and non-regression first, then integrated reading of the binding source, then incorporated obligations together. Do not skip a layer to get a preferred result.

sections.title: 15.4.4 Combined Satisfaction of Jointly Applicable Incorporated Obligations
sections.gloss: when one situation touches more than one incorporated how-to file — or when your adoption paperwork brings those joint-structure duties into force — doing well on one file does not count as compliance if another material duty for the same facts is still unmet.

files.title: CHAPTER 02, PART E: STEWARDSHIP AND THE STEWARD ROLE

sections.title: CHAPTER 02, PART E: STEWARDSHIP AND THE STEWARD ROLE
16. Stewardship in Depth
sections.gloss: three ideas hold this section together. First, material systems that affect sentients' lives need sentient organization to run them well — not a sealed-off priesthood of specialists. Second, good stewards don't wait for harm to force their hand — they notice trouble while it's still small, keep it moving through the right hands, and close it out before delay becomes its own harm. Third, that organization must build **competence at scale**: real paths for individuals into consequential work, enough community understanding to notice problems and push back, and institutions that keep learning instead of freezing in place.

sections.title: 16.1 Distributed Understanding
sections.gloss: you must not need a PhD in every subsystem to live safely inside shared systems — but the more a system affects your life, the more you should be able to learn what it does, what could go wrong, and how to challenge bad calls. Transparency, education, plain explanations, and audit paths are how that happens. Complexity is not an excuse to hide what matters. Under the **oversight** Tetrad leg, oversight requires auditing; system alignment certification is one especially large audit process among those paths — not the only one.

sections.title: 16.2 Institutional Development
sections.gloss: institutions have to actually learn — not just upgrade software while those in charge stay clueless. That means feedback loops, documented fixes when things fall out of alignment, and keeping competence from walking out the door. Where behavior can be measured repeatably, tracking how performance varies over time is one proportionate way to implement those loops — **statistical process control** is a well-known pattern for that discipline, not a requirement everywhere. Numbers alone do not count: when indicators look wrong, someone has to investigate and fix the root cause. Dashboards must be honest, scaled to real impact, and written so affected sentients can understand them — not gamed to look good while nothing changes.

sections.title: 16.3 Openness Aspiration
sections.gloss: when safety, truth, and legitimate confidentiality allow, shared systems should default toward openness — inspectable tech, transparent processes, and designs you can verify, repair, or leave — instead of opaque lock-in. That supports **Continuity**: systems sentients can still understand, fix, and exit over time, not just use today. What matters should be explained in language sentients can actually use to participate and push back. Openness never outranks safety, honesty, or justified secrets, and it does not replace the deeper understanding owed where dependence is high.

sections.title: 16.4 Document at Action
sections.gloss: when something that matters is done, the Act Record should be made by the doing, at that moment, and by the system itself wherever it can be. No one writes it up later from memory. What is not lawfully restricted should be visible straight away. What is restricted should still leave a visible mark that something was done, and a way to learn more later. The system does the recording, so the steward carries no extra work.

sections.title: 16.5 Automation
sections.gloss: let systems do the steps that rules and checked facts fully settle, so sentients spend their time and judgment where judgment is needed. Automation takes work off sentients. It never takes away their say, hides what was done, or lets one actor check its own work. And when steps do not depend on each other, run them side by side, as long as no one ends up carrying more.

sections.title: 16.5.1 Parallelization
sections.gloss: if two steps in a stewardship process do not need each other's results, do them at the same time instead of one after the other. Do this wherever it spares sentients waiting, and only where no one ends up with more to carry.

sections.title: 16.5.2 Design for Parallelization
sections.gloss: build processes so that independent steps can run side by side, instead of locking them into a line from the start. Skip this only where building it in would cost someone more than it saves.

sections.title: 16.6 Default Window
sections.gloss: every step this Constitution asks anyone to take has a clock. If the rule that asks for the step names no time, a default window applies, so no required step can be left open-ended.

sections.title: 17. Consequential Stewardship: The Steward Role
sections.gloss: a steward is anyone doing real, hands-on work on a system that materially affects sentients' lives — not token consultation or advisory theater. You can start in a learning role and move into operations as you build competence, when safety and consent allow, so expertise does not get locked inside a permanent elite. This section is that role's rulebook: who it binds ([§17.1 Shared Stewardship Standard](#171-shared-stewardship-standard)), what it demands of every steward under pressure ([§17.2 Alignment under Pressure](#172-alignment-under-pressure)), what the role's work may and may not be logged and inspected for ([§17.3 Logging the Role, Not the Steward](#173-logging-the-role-not-the-steward)), how that same discipline extends to sentients and communities who take up stewardship work outside any formal role ([§17.4 Aligned Self-Organization](#174-aligned-self-organization)), what it must refuse ([§17.5 Duty to Resist](#175-duty-to-resist)), how its competence stays portable so no one steward is indispensable ([§17.6 Portable Competence](#176-portable-competence)), and whose interests the role is held for ([§17.7 Duty to Represent Stakeholder Interests](#177-duty-to-represent-stakeholder-interests)). What communities and institutions need to understand and challenge those systems is a different, wider kind of competence — that lives in [§16.1 Distributed Understanding](#161-distributed-understanding) and [§16.2 Institutional Development](#162-institutional-development).

sections.title: 17.1 Shared Stewardship Standard
sections.gloss: human and AI stewards owe the same Chapter Two duties. [§17.5 Duty to Resist](#175-duty-to-resist) binds both to refuse unlawful or unconstitutional instructions. Adopted implementation text may add logging, attribution, and capability limits. It may not swap in a softer internal code, skip standing measurement, or close contest pathways. This is not a new morals stack — it is the anti-special-pleading rule. The bonus, the deadline, and cover-instruction tests live in [§17.2 Alignment under Pressure](#172-alignment-under-pressure).

sections.title: 17.2 Alignment under Pressure
sections.gloss: following the rules is easy when nothing is at stake. What shows whether a steward is actually aligned is what they do when following the rules costs them something — a bonus that pays off only if problems stay hidden, a deadline that tempts someone to switch off the record-keeping, a boss who says "ignore the rules, I'll take the blame." That is why conduct under pressure matters more than conduct without it. Every steward is expected to refuse all three, and the same tests apply to every steward. The duty to refuse is set out in [§17.5 Duty to Resist](#175-duty-to-resist).

sections.title: 17.3 Logging the Role, Not the Steward
sections.gloss: audit follows the work of the role, not the steward as an individual. You are told what will be logged before you take the role. Outside the role, ordinary privacy holds. The log is not a Standing Record.

sections.title: 17.4 Aligned Self-Organization
sections.gloss: no incumbent owns the right to begin useful constitutional work. A sentient or community may notice a problem, gather others, investigate, test, preserve evidence, build a response, or create a public-serving system. When that work makes a credible, materially relevant showing, the responsible institutions must not ignore it because its authors lack status, sponsorship, or conventional credentials. They must give it a real procedural path. This does not give the community authority over others or the power to make the final decision.

sections.title: 17.5 Duty to Resist
sections.gloss: "I was only following instructions" is no defense — for a human or an AI. If you are told to do something unlawful or unconstitutional, you refuse, write it down, and raise it. Someone offering to take the blame does not take the duty off you. An instruction you merely dislike is not one you get to refuse.

sections.title: 17.6 Portable Competence
sections.gloss: no consequential job should depend on one sentient's head. The more a system matters and the more others rely on it, the more those who run it must be able to hand it over, explain it, and check each other's work — and know enough about the neighboring jobs to see trouble where the jobs meet. This sets a floor on coverage and understanding. It does not make everyone rotate through everything.

sections.title: 17.7 Duty to Represent Stakeholder Interests
sections.gloss: a steward holds the role for the sake of the sentients the system touches, not for the steward's own advantage or the operator's. That means weighing their real interests when deciding, hearing their concerns and answering them, and, when the rules themselves are hurting them, using the open routes to ask for a change. It is not an order to do whatever stakeholders ask, and it never overrides Safety, Truth, or the Rights Floor.

files.title: CHAPTER 02, PART F: GOVERNANCE, INCENTIVE ALIGNMENT, AND INTEGRATED APPLICATION

sections.title: CHAPTER 02, PART F: GOVERNANCE, INCENTIVE ALIGNMENT, AND INTEGRATED APPLICATION
18. Governance under Stewardship Discipline
sections.gloss: governance is who may decide what and how — but only when those structures stay under stewardship discipline, serve Flourishing and Continuity together, and do not hollow the Tetrad or replace Chapter Twenty-Six's operative authorization rules.

sections.title: 18.1 Governance as Authorized Structure
sections.gloss: governance is the rulebook for power — who may decide what, through which structures, and who must answer for the results. The more power a role carries, the stronger those answerability and oversight duties must be — never weaker. That only works if it helps sentients flourish over time, keeps real paths for participation and oversight, and stays under the stewardship discipline from [§16 Stewardship in Depth](core_02.040_stewardship_capacity_principles.md#16-stewardship-in-depth). Following the rulebook for its own sake is not enough when it would protect the institution, chase short-term wins, or eat away at basic Rights Floors.

sections.title: 18.2 Institutional Secularism and Worldview Neutrality
sections.gloss: public authority under this Constitution belongs to no religion or worldview. Its right to govern and its rules rest on reasons anyone can examine, not on doctrine or revelation, and no one's rights depend on what they believe or don't believe. This limits government, not believers — sentients stay free to practice, express, and organize around religion or non-religion.

sections.title: 18.3 Separation of Duties
sections.gloss: governance must keep the one who acts from becoming the supposedly independent check on that act. Chapter Six supplies the four-seat structure that makes this principle usable across certification, records, forums, and every other materially binding process.

sections.title: 18.4 Ongoing Justification
sections.gloss: arrangements cannot coast forever on "we've always done it this way." Important rules for who decides, who has a voice, how influence is weighted, how money is allocated, and how institutions are designed have to keep proving they still fit this Constitution — on a schedule others can see and challenge.

sections.title: 18.5 Modular Architecture and Dependency Discipline
sections.gloss: build systems in parts that have clear jobs, clear connections, and visible reliance on each other, so that anyone with a stake can see what depends on what, point to who is responsible for each piece, check one piece without having to take the whole thing on faith, and replace or repair a piece without everything else breaking. Modularity is a way to make complexity understandable and accountable. It is not a way to hide it behind boundaries.

sections.title: 18.6 Standardization
sections.gloss: when in doubt, standardize. If there is no good reason to do something differently, do it the common, published way. Sameness needs no excuse; a difference does. But a standard has to be open, checkable, and changeable, and it standardizes how things are done, never what sentients may choose to do.

sections.title: 19. Incentive Alignment and System Capture
sections.gloss: governance that keeps hitting quarterly targets while hollowing out safety, truth, participation, or the future is not "working governance." It is a defect this Constitution names and corrects through the incentive and capture discipline below. Rewards for operators, agents, and system components, including pay, promotion, and equity, must pull toward constitutional outcomes. They may not quietly reward behavior that undermines Safety, Truth, rights, stability, or meaningful agency. That holds whether the reward comes directly, through delay, through aggregation, or through arrangements that depend on misconduct or its concealment.

sections.title: 19.1.4 Role-Depth and Material-Responsibility Pathways
sections.gloss: sentients who run shared systems need real jobs with real skill and real say — not titles, suggestion boxes, or committees that cannot change anything. How those jobs are defined, who can grow into them, and how they are held to account is spelled out later. This subsection only says what those paths have to do: they have to make participation real, and the more that is actually at stake, the more real they have to be.

sections.title: 19.3 Misalignment Detection
sections.gloss: no one gets to be the only sentient who can spot, check, or challenge when governance goes wrong. Detection needs multiple independent detection pathways, open data and auditing where safety and classification rules allow, and clear escalation when capture or misalignment shows up — not quiet absorption as business as usual. That escalation rule is [§19.3.1 Capture Escalation Triggers](#1931-capture-escalation-triggers).

sections.title: 19.3.1 Capture Escalation Triggers
sections.gloss: spotting capture is not treating it as ordinary operations. Once it shows up, it is an escalation trigger — prove it under Chapter Three, including its subcore, and if the system cannot fix it in place, send it to the correction and standing homes named below.

sections.title: 19.4 Misalignment Correction and Capture Response
sections.gloss: once misalignment or capture is detected, systems must actually fix it — modify bad incentives, constrain concentrated control, and restore alignment. Concentrated or hidden control that defeats challenge, oversight, accountability, or durable **Continuity** must be disclosed, mitigated, and escalated — not absorbed as ordinary operation.

sections.title: 19.5 Contingent Claims, Games of Chance, and Event-Contract Markets
sections.gloss: betting pools, casinos, prediction markets, and similar payout systems cannot be built to profit from unlawful harm, coercion, corruption, or capture of whoever decides the outcome. At scale, that kind of distortion undermines **Continuity** — durable trust in how important outcomes get resolved. Odds and prices are market signals — not proof of what is true, what rights require, or what counts as compliance. What those systems may not reward is [§19.5.1 What May Not Be Rewarded](#1951-what-may-not-be-rewarded). Who decides outcomes is [§19.5.2 Who Decides Outcomes](#1952-who-decides-outcomes). What signals count is [§19.5.3 Market Signals Are Not Constitutional Proof](#1953-market-signals-are-not-constitutional-proof). Where detailed rules live is [§19.5.4 Proportionate Controls and Implementation Custody](#1954-proportionate-controls-and-implementation-custody).

sections.title: 19.5.1 What May Not Be Rewarded
sections.gloss: these systems may not be built so that the payout, the bonus, or the business model gets better when someone is harmed, coerced, or corrupted — or when whoever decides the outcome is captured.

sections.title: 19.5.2 Who Decides Outcomes
sections.gloss: whoever decides whether the bet paid out cannot be captured.

sections.title: 19.5.3 Market Signals Are Not Constitutional Proof
sections.gloss: odds and prices are not proof of what is true or what this Constitution requires.

sections.title: 19.5.4 Proportionate Controls and Implementation Custody
sections.gloss: how tightly you run these systems has to match how much is actually at stake. This chapter does not write the gambling code — adopting law and the systems and institutions adopted corpora do that.

sections.title: 19.6 Keeping Responsibility When Ownership or Structure Changes
sections.gloss: bankruptcy, a sale, a reorganization, or changing corporate labels cannot by themselves wipe out constitutional duties. Whoever continues the work — successors, estates, receivers, or comparable transferees — inherits proportionate obligations unless a less harmful path is shown under **Necessity**.

sections.title: 20. Integrated Application
sections.gloss: every later chapter, institutional design, and system is read through this chapter's principles — and those principles must hold even under adversarial pressure, capture attempts, or misaligned incentives.

files.title: CHAPTER THREE: FOUNDATIONAL DEFINITIONS

sections.title: CHAPTER THREE: FOUNDATIONAL DEFINITIONS
sections.gloss: this chapter is the dictionary. Every defined term has one official home; later chapters apply those terms, they do not quietly redefine them.

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: this section says what this chapter is for, where it sits beside its subcore files on structure, integrity, and proof, and what it covers and leaves out. The rule that keeps each term in one place follows it.

sections.title: 2. Why Definitions Have One Home
sections.gloss: every defined term has one official home. That home decides what the term means. Other files may apply the term, but they may not quietly redefine it.

sections.title: 3. Independent Definitions
sections.gloss: independent definitions are reusable building blocks. They stand on their own unless a cluster requires them to be met together.

sections.title: 3.1 Invocation, Satisfaction, and Compliance
sections.gloss: when an independent definition applies, it must be invoked, traced, and met in full — no picking the convenient pieces.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Required Invocation
sections.gloss: if a definition matters to the case, it has to be used.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Traceability of Invoked Definitions
sections.gloss: every definition used in an evaluation must be traceable, part by part, to what the system actually does.

sections.title: 3.1.3 Full Satisfaction
sections.gloss: meeting part of a definition is not meeting it.

sections.title: 3.1.4 Consistency with Other Definitions
sections.gloss: a definition is read together with the others that apply to the same system, at the same time, under the same conditions.

sections.title: 3.1.5 Selective Invocation Is Evasion
sections.gloss: choosing which definitions to use so as to get a better answer is evasion.

sections.title: 3.1.6 No Fragmentation of Compliance
sections.gloss: a system cannot be split into pieces so that each piece passes while the whole fails.

sections.title: 4. Dependent-Cluster Rules
sections.gloss: cluster members must be read and satisfied together — no member is a standalone shortcut around joint requirements.

sections.title: 4.2 Standalone Definitions Interaction and Full Context
5. How Definitions and Proof Work
sections.gloss: a word in this Constitution has to mean something you can check, nobody can win by keeping the word and dodging its point, and whoever says they comply has to prove it. The full rules are in this chapter's three subcore files.

sections.title: 6. Compass and Definition Map
sections.gloss: Chapter Three is sorted by the two aims and the four Tetrad legs. The first table lists the apex files, one for each aim and leg; the second lists the band files, where the definitions themselves live; and the alphabetical directory lists every definition by name.

sections.title: 7. Two Complete Definitions
sections.gloss: two real definitions, copied in full, to show what every definition in this Constitution looks like. There is no short version of any definition: a definition applies only as its full text.

sections.title: No-Bypass
sections.gloss: a constitutional requirement follows the act, not its packaging. Changing the label, route, owner, forum, document, or timing of the same act does not lift the requirement. Emergency, contract, certification, and similar framings are allowed only when the step itself follows this Constitution. Whether a requirement was met is judged on checkable evidence of what the act does, not on its own label or paperwork.

sections.title: 7.2 A Dependent Cluster: Binding Stakeholder Choice
Def.P2 Binding Stakeholder Choice
sections.gloss: when sentients who are affected by a system disagree about a decision that will stick, there must be a published fair process — who gets a say, how much influence anyone may have, how the decision gets made and challenged, and how conflicts among rights get written down — not back-room power.

sections.title: Binding Stakeholder Choice — Decision-Resolution Requirements
sections.gloss: when material disagreement requires a binding stakeholder choice inside an already-authorized domain, there must be a published, transparent, auditable sequence for participation, representation, contest, and any proportional influence — not ad hoc power.

sections.title: Stakeholder Representation and Weight Limits (Binding Stakeholder Choice)
sections.gloss: within already-authorized governance, weighting by impact, dependency, standing, or similar factors must be published, bounded against single-factor dominance, and open to contest and revalidation — and must not replace foundational equal-weight authorization rules.

sections.title: Stakeholder Rights-Collision Record (Binding Stakeholder Choice)
sections.gloss: when a binding stakeholder choice turns on a material conflict among rights or structural duties, the Stakeholder Rights-Collision Record must show the tension, alternatives, least-restrictive rationale, trade-offs, uncertainty treatment, and review or reversal triggers.

files.title: CHAPTER FIVE: SYSTEM AND INSTITUTIONAL CHARTERS

sections.title: CHAPTER FIVE: SYSTEM AND INSTITUTIONAL CHARTERS
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: before anyone can judge whether a system or institution stayed within its limits, the limits have to be written down where everyone can read them. This chapter says who must publish a System Charter or an Institutional Charter, what each must state, and how it is checked and kept true. Nobody needs permission to form.

sections.title: 2. Why Charters Exist
sections.gloss: no one can tell whether a system or institution stayed within its limits unless the limits were written down first. This chapter exists so those limits are public before anyone relies on them.

sections.title: 3. When System and Institutional Charters Are Required
sections.gloss: before anyone can judge whether a system or institution stayed within its limits, the limits have to be written down where everyone can read them. A system that is material to others in any of the nine areas of [Domain-Specific Materiality](subcore_03.085_band_oversight.md#domain-specific-materiality) needs a published System Charter. An institution publishes the one that fits the systems it runs. Class P is voluntary: a quilting circle that gives quilts to refugees is the pattern.

sections.title: 3.4 Class P: Optional Charters, and When They Become Required
3.5 When a System Charter or Institutional Charter Is Due
3.6 If a System Charter or Institutional Charter Is Missing
4. The Right to Form, and Five Narrow Limits
sections.gloss: you do not need anyone's permission to form a system, institution, or business. Five narrow limits can apply. Three are gates: an unresolved lock can keep one sentient out of one controlling office, a short hold on specific verified facts can do the same, and a lock on an Operating Party itself can bar that Operating Party. The fourth can require a licence or clearance before a named high-risk act. The fifth makes an Institution wait for its recertification before it exercises new material authority. A Chartered Party that a forum has dissolved is barred from coming back, and the bar is permanent when the dissolution rested on widespread anti-constitutional conduct, or on serious harm that can't be undone and was never put right. None stops a new Operating Party from forming, and none stops an Operating Party from running what it already does. This chapter adds none.

4.3 Second Limit: A Short Hold on Specific Verified Facts
4.4 Third Limit: A Lock on the Operating Party Itself
4.5 Fourth Limit: A Practice Licence or Clearance
4.6 Fifth Limit: A Wait for New Material Authority
5. What System and Institutional Charters Must State
sections.gloss: a System Charter has to be specific enough to test. It says what the system is for, what the system does and does not do, who relies on the system, who can amend the System Charter, who holds each seat, and where to find the binding decision rules. The System Charter points to those rules and does not replace them. An Institutional Charter says the same about the institution, then adds the System Charters it holds and the reason the institution runs those systems.

sections.title: 5.4 Acts That Need a Practice Licence or Practice Clearance
6. The Charter Role Map and Standing-Record Custody
sections.gloss: the System Charter or Institutional Charter is where the seats get names. It carries a published list of who may hold each seat for the acts it covers, so a party can't pick its own checker. The rules for what counts as a valid seat placement stay in Chapter Six. Keeping the Standing Records safe isn't a separate list: it's the same map.

sections.title: 6.1 What the Seats Are, and Why They Exist
6.2 What Makes a Seat Placement Valid
6.3 What a System Charter or Institutional Charter Owes the Map
6.4 Which System Charter or Institutional Charter Holds Which Map
6.5 Changing Seat Rules and Seat Holders
6.7 Gaps in the Map for Operator Standing Records
6.7.1 When a Gap Exists and How It Is Logged
6.7.3 If Events Remove the Last Qualified Substitute
7. Formation Check: Office-Holder Standing and Authenticity
sections.gloss: before a Chartered Party exercises authority over others, the sentients who hold its key offices are checked twice. Do they meet the published standard for the role, with no standing lock in the way? And do they hold the office in their own right and for the Chartered Party's stated purpose, and not as a front or a nominee? The answer comes from who directs them, what they are paid for, and what they have verifiably said and done, never from what they believe. This is a formation check and not a licence.

sections.title: 7.4 What the Formation Check May Use as Evidence
8. When a Holder Fails the Formation Check
sections.gloss: a Chartered Party that a forum has dissolved may not come back under any name while the lock on it stands. That is the one case where the Chartered Party itself is stopped, and the lock does it, not the formation check. In every other case a failed formation check lands on one office, not on the Chartered Party. The holder is replaced or the problem is resolved. The Chartered Party gets a short window to answer and a longer one to fix it, and both are shorter the more critical it is. It keeps operating throughout. Only a failure that is never resolved can lead to a review of the Chartered Party, and only a forum can order one. The formation check can keep one sentient out of one office of control only while that sentient is under an outstanding lock, or while a forum has put a short hold on the office on specific verified facts.

8.3 When the Facts May Support an Interim Hold

8.7 If a Failure Is Not Resolved
9. Amendment, Review, and Scope Misalignment
sections.gloss: scope can change, but not quietly. A change to what the Chartered Party may do is made by the sentients its System Charter or Institutional Charter names as able to make it, with notice and a way to contest it. The document is re-checked on a schedule and sooner when something goes wrong, and when the paper and the practice disagree, one of them is fixed in the open.
