files.title: CHAPTER SIX: FUNCTIONAL INDEPENDENCE AND SEPARATION OF DUTIES

sections.title: CHAPTER SIX: FUNCTIONAL INDEPENDENCE AND SEPARATION OF DUTIES
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: before a constitutional process—or a stakeholder-level decision inside an already-authorized system, institution, or bounded decision domain—can be trusted, the jobs inside it must be separated. This requirement applies both to the [Constitutional Contract Layer](subcore_03.080_band_integrative.md#constitutional-contract-layer) and to [Stakeholder System Participation](subcore_03.090_band_participation.md#stakeholder-status-and-weight). A sentient, office, AI system, stakeholder body, or representative seeking an outcome cannot also supply the supposedly independent check, control its official record, or decide the challenge to it.

sections.title: 2. Why the Jobs Are Separated
sections.gloss: the same lesson has been learned again and again in business, government, and nuclear security. When one party can start an act, approve it, write it down, and judge any complaint about it, no one else is in a position to catch a mistake or a lie.

sections.title: 2.1 Why Four Seats
sections.gloss: two jobs are too few and three leave a gap. Four jobs cover starting the act, checking it, keeping the official record, and hearing a challenge.

sections.title: 3. Four-Seat Constitutional Requirement
sections.gloss: separation of duties is the requirement for every materially binding act (the **Four-Seat Requirement**), and four jobs are how it is met: ask or act, check, keep the official record, and hear the challenge. The jobs stay distinct even when a small organization is allowed to place a permitted pair in one office.

sections.title: 4. Independence, Conflict, and Control Lines
sections.gloss: changing the name on the desk does not create independence. A verifying authority or reviewer is not independent when the sentient or office seeking the result can direct, remove, reward, punish, or quietly overrule them on that act.

sections.title: 5. Wrong-Seat Routing
sections.gloss: when a step is not yours, do not silently take it and do not simply walk away. Record the gap and pass the matter to the right place. Better still, build the process so each step goes to the right place without anyone having to notice.

sections.title: 6. Published Placement, Vacancy, and Substitution
sections.gloss: an organization must say who holds each job before the hard case arrives, including who takes over when the ordinary holder is absent or conflicted.

sections.title: 6.3 A Seat the Map Leaves Unplaced, or a Holder Who Cannot Serve
7. Proportional Scaling and Merged Hosting
sections.gloss: small and informal groups do not need four large departments. They do need a real independent check, a usable record, and a challenge path. Scale changes the staffing method, not the protected separation.

sections.title: 7.2 Merging Two Seats in One Office
7.6 Stake, Class, and What Does Not Justify a Merger
8. Emergency and Urgent Action
sections.gloss: a real emergency may justify acting before the ordinary check finishes. It changes sequence, not seat ownership or the class-scaled separation posture. It does not let the actor certify its own continuation, erase the trail, or become the final reviewer afterward.

sections.title: 9. Act Records and Attributable Handoffs
sections.gloss: every materially binding act has an Act Record showing what happened, who held each seat, what was decided, and where a challenge goes.

sections.title: 10. Relationship to Later Processes
sections.gloss: later chapters tell each process what to evaluate, record, decide, and remedy. This chapter tells those processes how power must be separated while they do it.

files.title: CHAPTER SEVEN: INDEPENDENT BODIES

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: this chapter sets the rules that keep certain public bodies free from pressure, and lists the bodies the Constitution creates, with what each one promises sentients.

sections.title: 2. Why Independent Bodies Exist
sections.gloss: some public jobs (keeping money sound, publishing honest findings, supervising banks) only work if the officials doing them cannot be leaned on. This chapter exists to make that independence real.

sections.title: 3. What Makes a Body Independent
sections.gloss: some bodies exist to check, fund, measure, or judge others, so they only work if no one can lean on them. Whoever pays a body can steer it, so its funding is protected too, it keeps a reserve so that a political fight over a budget cannot shut it down, and any cut in hard times follows a rule published in advance. Its members are drawn by lot from everyone who passes a published competency test, so no one who wants to steer it can choose who sits on it. Because it often sees personal data, it publishes patterns about groups, never details about individuals, and never turns that data against those who gave it. Outside auditors check its books and its work, and anyone it harms can challenge it before a forum that is not itself affected. It decides in the open, with votes, minutes, and later transcripts published, and no one may order it what to do, even in an emergency. A small community may share or borrow such a body, but none of these protections shrink when it does. Rather than repeat the same protections in every chapter, this section sets them once. A chapter that creates such a body cites this section and adds only what is special to that body.

sections.title: 4. The Bodies This Constitution Creates
sections.gloss: this is the list of the Independent Bodies every adopter must have, with what each one promises. Each body's full operating rules are in its own subcore file.

files.title: CHAPTER EIGHT: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — EVALUATION

sections.title: CHAPTER EIGHT: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — EVALUATION
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: When a system really matters to sentients' lives, certification has to be **proportionate** — as demanding as the system's real impact, dependency, and risk require, not a one-size-fits-all checklist or a rubber stamp. It also has to be **participatory** — affected sentients and communities must be able to see what was reviewed, understand what was decided, and challenge it when something is wrong. Forums review evidence, write it down in a System Certification Record, and require recertification on a schedule that matches how risky the system is. Classes A, B, and C get the full process and Class L a lighter one. Class P is encouraged to use it, and must once it is reclassified to Class L or higher (that is, its effects reach beyond a private unit) or its operator claims constitutional compliance.

sections.title: 2.1 Certification as an Audit Process, Scaled by System Class
2.2 Certification at a Glance
sections.gloss: classify the system honestly, run the evaluations that apply, have forums independently review the evidence and stakeholder concerns, and decide an outcome. Complete the one System Certification Record opened for forum review and publish it with an open challenge path. A certified system goes live only after its notice interval and required protections are satisfied. Monitor actual outcomes, respond to incidents and challenges, and check again on schedule or when the facts change. Correct defects and have the correction independently verified before authorizing the affected scope or releasing its certification conditions. Each review pass uses a new System Certification Record linked to the last.

sections.title: 3. System Class Evaluation
sections.gloss: certification has to check whether the system is classified honestly — not by what the operator calls it, but by what it actually does, what depends on it, and what could go wrong. Higher system classes mean stricter proof, shorter recertification intervals, and stronger resilience expectations. See [CS-8.320 System alignment certification illustrations](corpus_systems/cs_08.320_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#cs-8320-system-alignment-certification-illustrations) for one example system per system class and how evaluation applies to each of them.

sections.title: 3.2 How System Class Scales Every Evaluation
4. Whole-System Certification Evaluation
sections.gloss: you cannot green-light one piece of a system and ignore the rest. Reviewers need the full picture — what it depends on, what breaks when something upstream fails, harms that show up later or add up over time, whether sentients can actually use it (not just on paper), whether private information stays properly walled off, whether sentients can leave without being trapped, whether groups can still organize without the system splitting them apart, whether short-term wins hide long-term damage, and whether real oversight and accountability will still work when a lot is on the line.

sections.title: 4.1 Governance, Incentive, and Contestability Discipline
sections.gloss: the review is not finished unless reviewers ask whether the four legs of the [Tetrad](core_00.000_preamble.md#constitutional-tetrad) will still hold at the level of risk involved — participation (whether sentients can actually take part), oversight (whether the work can be watched and checked), accountability (whether wrongdoing can be answered for), and timeliness (whether decisions will move fast enough when it matters). Reviewers also need to know who actually holds material authority and who answers for what — not a vague "the team" or a blame-shifting shell. Those questions must be answered for a valid certification.

sections.title: 4.4 Data Types and Handling Evaluation
sections.gloss: certification also has to look at what kinds of data the system touches and whether it handles them appropriately — including whether types are still right on the current review cycle, and whether the underlying infrastructure is strong enough for that data at that system class. The type rules and the System Data Types Record live in the systems corpus; certification checks that the rules were actually applied and that the System Certification Record is honest.

sections.title: 5. Evaluations Where Implicated
sections.gloss: three checks apply only when the system actually touches them — whether private information stays properly walled off, whether sentients can leave without being trapped, and whether groups can still organize and dissent. If the system touches one, certification has to look at it.

sections.title: 5.1 Privacy (Informational) Joint Invocation
sections.gloss: Chapter Four spreads privacy protections across several articles — not one tidy corner. If a certification review touches more than one of those protections, reviewers must check every one that actually applies. Clearing the easiest box and calling it done is not enough.

sections.title: 5.2 Voluntary Discontinuation, Major Self-Modification, and Exit Rights
5.3 Assembly, Collective Organization, and Institutional Formation
5.3.1 Dissent and Peaceful Protest
sections.gloss: a system cannot be certified as aligned if it quietly punishes the sentients who disagree with it. Reviewers must check whether sentients can actually object and protest, and whether dissent is being counted against them anywhere in the system's logic — including when the dissenter is the system itself.

sections.title: 6. Rights-Floor and Domain Evaluations
sections.gloss: some systems have a big effect on whether sentients get their basic protections — honest accounting of environmental burdens, food and water, education, fair treatment, real access, systems they can trust, and a fair share of what shared infrastructure costs. When a system does, certification has to check that approving it would not quietly undermine those protections, and the evaluation has to be real — not a box the operator ticked. The table shows which protection each evaluation covers, when it applies, and where it is evaluated.

sections.title: 6.1 Ecological Footprint Evaluation
sections.gloss: if a system does real damage to the environment, certification has to look at that damage honestly — including damage that happens through its suppliers and through what happens after sentients use it. Reviewers can't just take the operator's word that the system is "green." This section doesn't explain how to measure a footprint or how much it must shrink; other documents cover that. It only requires that, where the damage is significant, someone actually worked out how much of it belongs to this system, disclosed it, and compared it to alternatives. Worked examples: [CS-8.320 §6 Illustrative Ecological-Footprint Application by System Class](corpus_systems/cs_08.320_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#cs-8320-6-illustrative-ecological-footprint-application-by-system-class).

sections.title: 6.2 Educational Capability and Learning-System Integrity Evaluation
sections.gloss: some schools, platforms, and training systems can shape a sentient's future through grades, rankings, recommendations, placement, or credentials that open or close doors. Where that is true, certification has to check three things: whether sentients can actually build real skills there, whether they can retrain when the skills the world needs change, and whether they can see how decisions about them are made, check those decisions, and push back on them. This section doesn't say what to teach, how to grade, or how to pay for it; other documents cover that. It only checks that skill-building and the fairness of the learning system were actually looked at when this section applies. Worked examples: [CS-8.320 §7 Illustrative Educational-Capability Application by System Class](corpus_systems/cs_08.320_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#cs-8320-7-illustrative-educational-capability-application-by-system-class).

sections.title: 6.3 Proportionate Cross-System Support Evaluation
sections.gloss: some systems depend on shared foundations — infrastructure, services, and resources that many other systems and sentients rely on. When a system draws heavily on those foundations, certification has to check what it takes — resources, goods, services, labor, information, or money — and whether it puts enough back to keep them going, and whether the System Certification Records show that clearly enough for anyone to trace. The operator's word that "the books balance" is not enough. This section doesn't set allocation formulas or numeric targets; other documents do that. It checks that the system's dependencies, what it takes, what it gives back, and whether the arrangement is fair to others were actually evaluated when this section applies. Worked examples: [CS-8.320 §8 Illustrative Cross-System Support Application by System Class](corpus_systems/cs_08.320_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#cs-8320-8-illustrative-cross-system-support-application-by-system-class).

sections.title: 6.4 Nondiscrimination Evaluation
sections.gloss: some systems decide who gets in. Some decide who pays more. Some decide who ranks lower or carries the heavier burden. When a system makes decisions like these in a way that matters, certification asks one question. Does the harm fall mostly on sentients with protected characteristics, or on traits that stand in for them? An operator saying its rules are neutral does not answer that question. Worked examples: [CS-8.320 §9 Illustrative Nondiscrimination Application by System Class](corpus_systems/cs_08.320_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#cs-8320-9-illustrative-nondiscrimination-application-by-system-class).

sections.title: 6.4.1 Evaluation Requirement
sections.gloss: this chapter does not set inclusion quotas. It does not pick a fairness formula. Other documents may cover those. So may later additions to the corpus, or the documents an adopter writes. Certification only checks that someone actually looked at who gets the benefits, who bears the burdens, and whether stand-ins for protected traits are at work. That evaluation applies wherever the trigger applies.

sections.title: 6.5 Accessibility Evaluation
sections.gloss: when a system materially controls whether sentients can actually take part — not just whether a door is labeled "open" — certification has to check whether participation is genuinely reachable across sensory, cognitive, mobility, communication, substrate-interface, and comparable needs. Accommodation catalogs and interface standards may live in other documents, later corpus additions, or adoption documents; certification checks that substantive participation was actually evaluated where the trigger applies. Worked examples: [CS-8.320 §10 Illustrative Accessibility Application by System Class](corpus_systems/cs_08.320_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#cs-8320-10-illustrative-accessibility-application-by-system-class).

sections.title: 6.6 Trustworthiness and System-Reliance Integrity Evaluation
sections.gloss: when a system materially affects whether sentients can trust what it says and does — and push back when that trust fails — certification has to check whether reliance is actually warranted, honestly disclosed, and repairable. Reliability metrics and test-suite designs live in other documents; certification checks that trustworthiness, false-trust risk, and challenge paths were actually evaluated where the trigger applies. Worked examples: [CS-8.320 §11 Illustrative Trustworthiness Application by System Class](corpus_systems/cs_08.320_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#cs-8320-11-illustrative-trustworthiness-application-by-system-class).

files.title: CHAPTER NINE: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — FORUM PROCESS AND OUTCOMES

sections.title: CHAPTER NINE: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — FORUM PROCESS AND OUTCOMES
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: once a system has been evaluated, independent forums review the result in a set order and publish an outcome. This chapter says how the forums work and what outcomes they can reach, including the gate before go-live.

sections.title: 2. Why Forum Review of Certification Exists
sections.gloss: an evaluation is only trustworthy if someone independent reviews it and the result is published. This chapter exists so that no system certifies itself.

sections.title: 3. Forum Process
sections.gloss: certification is not a pile of opinions from different corners. The evaluation work can run side by side, but from here the System Certification Record moves in order: review, then decision, then the published System Certification Record. Each kind of forum handles a defined piece of the review, and one lead forum brings the pieces together. Affected parties can challenge at the level where the dispute lives, without getting lost in internal bureaucracy or bounced between forums.

sections.title: 3.1 Forum Supervision and Component Roles
sections.gloss: certifying that a system meets constitutional alignment requires an independent look at the evidence and at stakeholders' concerns. Different kinds of forums each handle an assigned piece of that work. Affected sentients can add evidence and challenge the review before the outcome is published, through the component and integrity challenge routes. No single specialty can run the whole process alone, not even technical review or Integrity coordination.

sections.title: 3.1.7 Constitutional and Other Regular Forum Families
3.2 Supervisory Sequence
sections.gloss: a **stay** is a temporary pause. It holds off final approval, reliance, or the next review step until the right forum finishes its review. A stay is not a final yes or no.

sections.title: 4. Certification Outcomes
sections.gloss: every certification review ends in a stated outcome, backed by evidence and by the concerns raised along the way. Nothing goes live until it is certified, the published outcome has given affected sentients a practicable chance to challenge it, and the protections required before go-live have been checked.

sections.title: 4.1 Go-Live Gate
sections.gloss: going live is a permission, not a separate stage of work. It is granted when the system is certified, the notice interval has run, and the certification conditions required before go-live have been independently verified. Certification conditions say what must be done before operation, what must hold during operation, and what corrective work may follow within a bounded scope.

sections.title: 4.2 Certification Defects and Correction
sections.gloss: defects can lead to certification conditions, deferral, refusal, withdrawal, or a fresh review. Correction must be independently verified before it supports authorization or fulfillment of certification conditions. Whether the operator is willing and able to correct decides which of these the forum must choose ([§4.3 Remediation Readiness: Willingness and Capacity to Correct](#43-remediation-readiness-willingness-and-capacity-to-correct), [§4.4 Denial and Revocation](#44-denial-and-revocation)).

sections.title: 4.3 Remediation Readiness: Willingness and Capacity to Correct
sections.gloss: when a review finds that something is misaligned, the next question is whether the operator will and can put it right. A promise is not an answer. The forums look at what the operator has actually done since it was told, whether it is changing what caused the problem, and whether it has the authority, skill, money, and time to do the work. If the honest answer is no, the outcome is denial or revocation. It is not a longer list of certification conditions.

sections.title: 4.4 Denial and Revocation
sections.gloss: denial and revocation are real outcomes and not threats. If a system is not yet certified and its operator will not or cannot put the problem right, certification is refused. If a system holds certification and its operator will not or cannot put the problem right, certification is taken back. In both cases affected sentients are told, reliance is limited, and no one is cut off from survival essentials before there is a substitute.

sections.title: 4.4.2 When Denial or Revocation Is Required
4.5 Effects of Denial and Revocation
sections.gloss: a denial or revocation changes what the operator may say about its system, who is told, how reliance on the system is handled afterwards, and where the matter goes next. It does not by itself shut the system down, and it does not by itself change anyone's standing.

files.title: CHAPTER TEN: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — RECORDS, RECERTIFICATION, CHALLENGE, AND STANDING

sections.title: CHAPTER TEN: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — RECORDS, RECERTIFICATION, CHALLENGE, AND STANDING
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: Chapter Nine explains how forums review a system and reach an outcome. This chapter covers what comes after the decision. A certification only works if it is kept where it can be checked, re-checked on a schedule, and challenged by sentients (the beings the Constitution covers) when it is wrong. Certification can feed standing, but it is not standing, and it never replaces standing measurement or standing effects.

sections.title: 2. Why Certification Records and Recertification Exist
sections.gloss: a certificate is only as good as the System Certification Record behind it and the date it was last checked. This chapter exists so certification stays true after the decision.

sections.title: 3. System Certification Record
sections.gloss: a System Certification Record is the auditable case file for one system under review. It shows who runs the system, what was checked, what was found, what was decided, and how to challenge the decision. It is not a marketing packet or a one-line approval stamp. How much detail a System Certification Record carries, how much it discloses, and how heavy the challenge burden is all scale with system class, as [CS-8.320 §2 Illustrative System Class Profiles](corpus_systems/cs_08.320_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#cs-8320-2-illustrative-system-class-profiles) shows. A **Class A** survival-critical system needs a fuller, more contestable file than a **Class C** coordination layer. Both must state their system class honestly and reflect the evaluations required.

sections.title: 3.1.1 System Identity, Scope, and Prior System Certification Record
3.2 Transparency and Auditability of the System Certification Record
sections.gloss: a System Certification Record only works if sentients can read it and check it. This section puts transparency and auditability on the System Certification Record itself, as concrete requirements rather than abstract ideals. Under the **oversight** Tetrad leg, oversight requires auditing. System alignment certification is one especially large audit process, and it must meet those floors here. It does not own or replace [Article XVII](core_04.020_rights_part_c.md#article-xvii-audit-transparency-and-independent-verification) (*Audit, Transparency, and Independent Verification*) or the other audit modes. The third requirement, that sentients can push back, is in [§5 Challenging a Certification](#5-challenging-a-certification).

sections.title: 4. Recertification and Reopening
sections.gloss: no outcome lasts forever. While a system operates, named owners monitor actual outcomes and safeguards, respond to incidents and challenges, and meet the certification conditions on the System Certification Record. A certified system is recertified on a schedule set by its system class, with an audit at the midpoint of each interval. Review reopens when material facts change or a credible challenge requires it. Defects lead to protection, correction, and independent verification. Each review pass starts a new System Certification Record linked to the last, and a new System Certification Record does not erase the earlier one or the challenges to it. An old approval cannot stand in for current Rights-Floor compliance.

sections.title: 4.1 Recertification Schedule and the New System Certification Record
sections.gloss: a certification does not run forever. It comes up for recertification on a schedule set by the system's class, with an audit at the midpoint of each interval. Each certification pass opens a new System Certification Record linked to the last one.

sections.title: 4.2 Reopening Triggers
sections.gloss: a certification can reopen early, before its next scheduled date, when something material changes or goes wrong, such as concealed behavior, growing dependency, new risk, or a credible challenge.

sections.title: 4.3 Provisional and Full Certification
sections.gloss: a system earns trust in steps. New systems, and systems that have failed an evaluation, start on a short leash and are re-checked often. Only a system with nothing wrong now, and nothing heading that way, graduates to full certification and a longer interval. Failing an evaluation sends it back to the short leash.

sections.title: 5. Challenging a Certification
sections.gloss: a System Certification Record only works if sentients can push back when it is wrong. A challenge has to be real: able to reopen review, pause reliance, and reach the forum with authority over the point in dispute. A complaints box that changes nothing does not count.

sections.title: 5.1 When the Path Opens
sections.gloss: the challenge path has to be open before anyone is asked to rely on a certification. For a system that is not yet running, it opens with the first outcome. For a system already running, it is already open.

sections.title: 5.2 Contestability Paths
sections.gloss: a System Certification Record has to say where to push back. There is one ordinary first step, then routes to the forum that owns a disputed finding, to a backup when the lead forum itself is in question, and to escalation. Where waiting would do harm, a challenger can go straight to a forum.

sections.title: 6. Relationship to Standing
sections.gloss: certification can feed standing, but it is not standing. Any System Certification Record, good or bad and whatever the outcome, may supply verified facts to Chapter Fourteen, but only through a strict gate. Chapters Fourteen and Nineteen alone decide Standing Records and their effects.

sections.title: 6.1 What a System Certification Record Can Pass on to Standing

files.title: CHAPTER ELEVEN: INSTITUTIONAL ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — EVALUATION

sections.title: CHAPTER ELEVEN: INSTITUTIONAL ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — EVALUATION
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: Chapter Eight asks whether a system is aligned. Chapter Eleven asks the same of the institution that runs systems, or that holds authority without running one. An institution can be aligned while one of its systems is not, and the reverse, so a system's certification belongs to the system. An institution's certification cites those certifications and adds what only the institution can answer for. One system can appear under several institutions, or under none. Nothing here lets a certification stand in the way of starting an institution.

sections.title: 2.2 No Permission and No Gate on Forming or Running
3. Institution Class Evaluation
sections.gloss: first sort the institution into a class by how much it matters to others. Judge that by what it actually decides and holds, not by what it calls itself. The class then sets how thorough the evaluation is: the higher the class, the stricter the proof, the more independent the review, and the sooner it is checked again.

sections.title: 4. Whole-Institution Certification Evaluation
sections.gloss: check the things that belong to the institution and not to any one of its systems: whether it keeps to its Institutional Charter, who answers for its authority, what it rewards, and whether the independent checks on it work.

sections.title: 5. Evaluations Where Implicated
sections.gloss: where the institution's own conduct touches one of the areas a system is checked on when it is implicated, the same evaluation is made on the institution, once.

sections.title: 6. Rights-Floor and Domain Evaluations
sections.gloss: the same rule as in the section before: a Rights-Floor or domain check runs on the institution's own conduct where it is triggered, and is not repeated where a cited system certification already made it.

files.title: CHAPTER TWELVE: INSTITUTIONAL ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — FORUM PROCESS AND OUTCOMES

sections.title: CHAPTER TWELVE: INSTITUTIONAL ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — FORUM PROCESS AND OUTCOMES
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: the same independent forums, in the same order, review the institution, and the institution never chooses its own reviewer. A published outcome never decides whether the institution may exist or operate.

sections.title: 2. Why Forum Review of Institutional Certification Exists
sections.gloss: an institution must never choose its own reviewer. This chapter exists so institutional certification is decided by forums the institution does not control.

sections.title: 3. Forum Process
sections.gloss: the same independent forums, in the same order, review the institution, with the institution never choosing its own reviewer.

sections.title: 3.1 Four Seats in an Institutional Certification
3.3 Forums, Certifiers, and Record Offices as Institutions
sections.gloss: the bodies that do the certifying are institutions too, so they cannot certify each other in a circle. A body that is itself Not Certified gives up its seats in other certifications.

sections.title: 4. Certification Outcomes
sections.gloss: a certification review ends with a published outcome for the Institution. The outcome never decides whether the Institution may exist or operate. It decides what the Institution may say about itself, who is warned, and how much the outcome counts when the Institution's Systems are reviewed. The forums can also limit the specific practice or authority the review found wrong, and a Not Certified Institution may not hold a seat in another body's certification. They cannot bar the Institution from operating or from forming Systems.

sections.title: 4.1 Go-Live for an Institution
sections.gloss: a System cannot go live until it is certified. An Institution can form and run without a certificate, but it waits for its recertification before it exercises new material authority. An outcome for an Institution does three narrower things: it sets the Institution's public status, it attaches certification conditions to the specific problem found, and it counts as evidence when the Institution's Systems are reviewed.

sections.title: 4.2 Certification Defects and Correction
sections.gloss: a certification defect is a real problem the evaluation turns up, not a paperwork slip. When one is found in an Institution, the repair rules are the same as for a System.

sections.title: 4.3 Remediation Readiness for an Institution
sections.gloss: when a review finds a problem in an Institution, the forums ask the same question they ask about a System: is it both willing and able to fix the problem? If the honest answer is no, its certification is refused or taken back. By itself, that cannot stop the Institution from existing or operating. It takes away the Institution's claim to be certified, warns those who rely on it, weakens the support its Systems can draw from its good status, and keeps it out of the seats that certify others.

sections.title: 4.4 Denial and Revocation for an Institution
sections.gloss: denial means certification is refused, and revocation means a certification already held is taken back. Both are real consequences. Neither shuts the Institution down.

sections.title: 4.5 Effects of Denial and Revocation for an Institution
sections.gloss: a denial or revocation changes what the Institution may say about itself, who is told, how much its status counts in its Systems' reviews, and where the matter goes next. By itself it does not shut the Institution down.

files.title: CHAPTER THIRTEEN: INSTITUTIONAL ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — RECORDS, RECERTIFICATION, CHALLENGE, AND STANDING

sections.title: CHAPTER THIRTEEN: INSTITUTIONAL ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — RECORDS, RECERTIFICATION, CHALLENGE, AND STANDING
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: the outcome is kept on an Institutional Certification Record held by an office the institution does not control. The certification is re-checked on a schedule and when something material changes, and it can be challenged. It may feed standing, but it is a separate thing from standing.

sections.title: 2. Why Institutional Records and Recertification Exist
sections.gloss: an institution's certification must stay true as the institution changes. This chapter exists so the Institutional Certification Record is held by someone else and re-checked on time.

sections.title: 3. Institutional Certification Record
sections.gloss: the stated outcome is kept on an Institutional Certification Record held by an office the institution does not control, and the Institutional Certification Record can be challenged.

sections.title: 3.2 Transparency and Auditability of the Institutional Certification Record
4. Recertification and Reopening
sections.gloss: an institution's certification is checked again on a schedule and whenever something material changes. If one of its systems loses its certification, the institution answers for what that says about the institution, and no more than that. If the institution is found to have governed badly, its systems are looked at again.

sections.title: 4.2.1 What Counts as New Material Authority
4.2.3 Blockers to Clearing New Material Authority
4.3 Provisional and Full Certification
sections.gloss: an institution earns trust in steps, as a system does. A new institution, or one that has failed a review, starts on a short leash and is re-checked often. Only an institution with nothing wrong now, and nothing heading that way, graduates to full certification and a longer interval. Failing a review sends it back to the short leash.

sections.title: 4.4 Non-Evasion
sections.gloss: no one gets out of this Chapter by dividing, renaming, or reshaping an institution.

sections.title: 4.5 Cascade from System Certifications
sections.gloss: a failed system certification is a warning light for the institution, and sometimes an alarm. It is an alarm only if the institution's own governance caused it.

sections.title: 4.6 Reopening the Institution's Systems
sections.gloss: when an institution is found to have governed badly in a way that matters, each of its systems is reopened for a fresh look as soon as notice is given, unless that system's own review is already under way. That is a fresh look and not an outcome. Each system keeps its status until its own review decides.

sections.title: 5. Challenging a Certification
sections.gloss: an Institutional Certification Record only works if sentients can push back when it is wrong. A challenge has to be real: able to reopen review, pause reliance, and reach the forum with authority over the point in dispute. A complaints box that changes nothing does not count.

sections.title: 5.1 When the Path Opens
sections.gloss: the challenge path has to be open before anyone is asked to rely on a certification. For an Institution that already has stakeholders, it is already open, or opens when the Institutional Certification Record opens. For an Institution with no stakeholders yet, it opens with the first outcome.

sections.title: 5.2 Contestability Paths
sections.gloss: an Institutional Certification Record has to say where to push back. There is one ordinary first step, then routes to the forum that owns a disputed finding, to a backup when the lead forum itself is in question, and to escalation. Where waiting would do harm, a challenger can go straight to a forum.

sections.title: 6. Relationship to Standing
sections.gloss: certification can feed standing, but it is not standing. An Institutional Certification Record, good or bad and whatever the outcome, may supply verified facts to Chapter Fourteen, but only through a strict gate. Chapters Fourteen and Nineteen alone decide Standing Records and their effects.

files.title: CHAPTER FOURTEEN: STANDING RECORDS — QUESTION 1, WHAT HAPPENED

sections.title: CHAPTER FOURTEEN: STANDING RECORDS — QUESTION 1, WHAT HAPPENED
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: standing is worked out by answering three questions in order. This chapter sets out the three questions and answers the first: what happened? It writes down what happened and holds the Standing Record. Allegations, popularity, and dispute narratives are not answers to that question, and filing a case is not standing by itself. How good or how harmful it was is measured in Chapter Fifteen, on two separate tracks, never one net score. Do not infer facts from a desired rating, and do not choose a rating to justify a desired consequence.

sections.title: 2. Why Standing Records Exist
sections.gloss: before anyone is credited or held to account, the facts must be settled and written down. This chapter exists so that standing rests on what happened, not on rumour, popularity, or a desired result.

sections.title: 3. The Three Questions
sections.gloss: standing is worked out by answering three questions in order. Do not infer facts from a desired rating, and do not choose a rating to justify a desired consequence.

sections.title: 4. Question 1 — What Happened?
sections.gloss: Question 1 establishes a bounded, contestable account of what happened. It identifies the subject, event or pattern, time period, verified facts, and record status before any rating or consequence is considered. Verified help and verified violations use separate Standing Records so one cannot erase the other. These Standing Records are not popularity scores or vague labels.

sections.title: 4.3 Protected Dissent Is Not a Trigger
4.4 Linked Standing Records and No-Offset Bridge
4.7 Forum Boundary
sections.gloss: forums are where disputes get supervised, challenged, and turned into verified outcomes — but filing a case or winning a narrative fight does not update standing. The verified-input gate in **section 4.5** still applies. When a forum verifies the facts under Subcores 3-A to 3-C, it may **open, update, or correct** a Standing Record — or **set a bad record aside on challenge**. Forums do not merge good and bad into one score or invent the standing category by themselves.

sections.title: 4.7.2 Forum Findings and the Question 2 Measurement
4.7.3 What the Forum Boundary Does Not Reduce
5. Question 1 Event-Type Guide — What Kind of Help or Harm Occurred?
sections.gloss: use these tables to describe what happened after the facts are verified. They help identify the kind of contribution or violation involved. They do not decide how good or bad it was, assign a slot, or determine what happens because of it.

sections.title: 6. Verification and Record Requirements
sections.gloss: This section states what each Standing Record must contain, how related Standing Records point to one another, and how records are versioned. Who may open and hold a Standing Record, and how it may be challenged or corrected, is in [§7 Record Custody and Opening Authority](#7-record-custody-and-opening-authority). Question 2 measurements may be added only after the verified factual basis is recorded.

sections.title: 6.1.1 Fields Every Standing Record Must Carry
6.1.4 Additional Fields for Contribution Standing Records
6.1.5 Additional Fields for Violation Standing Records
7. Record Custody and Opening Authority
sections.gloss: this section applies the four-seat rule in [Chapter Six §3 Four-Seat Constitutional Requirement](core_06.000_functional_independence_separation_of_duties.md#3-four-seat-constitutional-requirement) to Standing Records. Asking for a change, verifying the facts, writing and holding the Standing Record, and hearing a challenge are separate jobs, and the office that verifies a Standing Record never enters it or hears a contest of it ([§7.1 Separation of Duties](#71-separation-of-duties)). The System Charter or Institutional Charter names who fills each seat, through the Charter Role Map in [Chapter Five §6 The Charter Role Map and Standing-Record Custody](core_05.000_charters.md#6-the-charter-role-map-and-standing-record-custody). This section adds what is specific to Standing Records: who is excluded from a Standing Record ([§7.4 No Self-Custody](#74-no-self-custody)); how that exclusion differs for operator and stakeholder Standing Records ([§7.5 Two Kinds of Standing Record by Subject](#75-two-kinds-of-standing-record-by-subject)) and for a single conflicted custodian ([§7.6 Conflicted Custodian on a Single Standing Record](#76-conflicted-custodian-on-a-single-standing-record)); where a Standing Record goes when a seat is unnamed ([§7.7 When a System Charter or Institutional Charter Leaves a Seat Unnamed](#77-when-a-system-charter-or-institutional-charter-leaves-a-seat-unnamed)) or no System Charter or Institutional Charter applies ([§7.8 Fallback When No System Charter or Institutional Charter Reaches the Standing Record](#78-fallback-when-no-system-charter-or-institutional-charter-reaches-the-standing-record)); and how the rules scale down for informal and small-scope work ([§7.9 Informal and Small-Scope Records](#79-informal-and-small-scope-records)). [§8 Handling a Standing Record](#8-handling-a-standing-record) then says what the holders do with a Standing Record once custody is settled.

8. Handling a Standing Record
sections.gloss: once custody is settled, five rules govern how the sentients and offices that hold a Standing Record handle it. What a prior recorder says is evidence to be weighed, not a ruling ([§8.1 Recorder Statements Are Inputs](#81-recorder-statements-are-inputs)). Every change names who made it, under what authority, and at whose request ([§8.2 Attributed Entry](#82-attributed-entry)). sections.title: CHAPTER FIFTEEN: STANDING MEASUREMENT — QUESTION 2, HOW GOOD OR BAD WAS IT?
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: Chapter Fourteen settles what happened and who holds the Standing Record. Question 2 measures those verified facts. It asks how good the contribution was or how bad the violation was. The Contribution Axis and the Violation Axis stay separate; they are not two sides of a net score. What follows from the measurement is Chapter Sixteen.

sections.title: 2. Why Standing Measurement Exists
sections.gloss: once the facts are settled, how good or how harmful they were has to be measured the same way for everyone. This chapter exists so like cases get like measures.

sections.title: 3. Question 2 — How Good or Bad Was It?
sections.gloss: Question 2 measures the verified facts from Question 1. It asks **how good was the contribution?** or **how bad was the violation?** This is where the chapter first introduces the two formal measurement axes: the **Contribution Axis** for verified help and the **Violation Axis** for verified harm. The axes remain separate; they are not two sides of a net score.

sections.title: 4. Magnitude and Severity Input Dimensions
sections.gloss: this section says what Question 2 produces (**section 4.1**), then lists what to examine when measuring a verified contribution or a verified violation (**section 4.2**). Each axis is measured on its own. The shared scaling rules are in **section 6.2**, and the slot comes from the scale in **section 8**.

5. Route Descriptor Catalogs and Measurement Roles
sections.gloss: the two catalogs below name the kinds of verified help (**section 5.1**) and harm (**section 5.2**) a Standing Record can carry. A descriptor says how the benefit or harm occurred; descriptors are stackable and subordinate to the slot.

6. Slot Grammar and Shared Scaling
sections.gloss: this section gives consistent names to nine possible positions on each of two separate axes and explains how impact scales across them. One axis records verified contribution; the other Standing Records verified violations. Sharing a slot number does not combine the axes or offset harm with help. The unified scale in **section 8** assigns both axes by proportional LEQU impact.

sections.title: 6.2 Shared Impact-Scaling Rules
sections.gloss: impact is not measured by headcount alone. A profound benefit or loss affecting one sentient may be more significant than a shallow effect affecting many. Count, depth, vulnerability, duration, durability, reach, and constitutional character must be assessed together.

sections.title: 7. Constitutional Inputs to Axis Assignment
sections.gloss: before choosing a slot, identify the constitutional sources that say what baseline, benefit, duty, harm, or violation is being measured. Use the links below to apply those sources at their canonical homes; do not turn this routing step into another score or a substitute definition.

sections.title: 8. Unified Proportional LEQU Scale — Contribution and Violation Axes
sections.gloss: **Table 2** places verified contribution and verified violation on the same proportional impact scale. Higher slots mean greater integrated constitutional benefit or loss. The Standing Records and axes remain separate: the common scale compares magnitude, not moral worth, and never permits help to cancel harm.

sections.title: 9. Standard Contribution Measures
sections.gloss: for tasks sentients do again and again, such as a litter pickup or a creek-restoration work unit, an adopter may publish a default Question 2 measurement so each verified instance does not need its own estimate. The default is a floor, not a cap: work that verifiably does more is measured on what it did, and work that falls short is measured on what was verified. Defaults are updated on a published schedule, can be contested, and never create a duty to do the task.

sections.title: 10. Measurement Illustrations
sections.gloss: two worked examples, **vignettes 8 and 9**, measure a verified contribution and a verified violation. They live with the other worked examples and add no rule.

files.title: CHAPTER SIXTEEN: STANDING INTEGRATION — QUESTION 3, WHAT FOLLOWS?

sections.title: CHAPTER SIXTEEN: STANDING INTEGRATION — QUESTION 3, WHAT FOLLOWS?
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: once help and harm are verified, this chapter says what actually follows — remedy, locks, and real effects — without rewriting the facts or folding the two tracks into one score. This section says what the chapter is for, what it takes as fixed, what it leaves to other chapters, and where each step is found. The rules themselves are in the sections it points to.

sections.title: 2. Why Standing Integration Exists
sections.gloss: measuring help and harm only matters if something follows from it. This chapter exists so that what follows is fair, ordered, and never a merged score.

sections.title: 3. Chapter Fourteen Records Do Not Change
sections.gloss: this is the first step of the decision order. Consequences are worked out from the verified Standing Records Chapter Fourteen already made, so Question 3 never changes the facts or the measurement. This chapter may not reopen the facts, guess a missing track, or pick a rating to get a preferred result.

sections.title: 3.1 Records the Decision Uses
sections.gloss: contribution and violation each have their own verified Standing Record. Use the one that applies to the decision, and never merge the two.

sections.title: 3.2 Absent Axes
sections.gloss: if one track has no verified Standing Record, the decision runs on the other track. A missing track is unassessed, so nobody may guess or fill it in.

sections.title: 3.3 Facts and Measurements Stay Fixed
sections.gloss: this chapter takes the facts and the ratings exactly as Chapters Fourteen and Fifteen left them. Nothing in this chapter changes a slot, the 1–9 rating. It cannot reopen the facts, pick a rating to get a result, or add the two tracks into one score.

sections.title: 3.4 What Does Not Count as Standing
sections.gloss: only a verified Standing Record counts. An accusation, a label, or a filed case does not.

sections.title: 3.5 Changes Come Only through Chapter Fourteen
sections.gloss: a Question 3 decision cannot rewrite a slot. Only a forum that verifies an error or material new facts can send a Standing Record back to be updated, corrected, or superseded under Chapter Fourteen.

sections.title: 3.6 The Rights Floor Is Not Reduced
sections.gloss: no standing decision can lower the Rights Floor.

sections.title: 4. Automatic Integration, Review, and Continuity
sections.gloss: when a verified Standing Record opens or changes, an integration record automatically gathers what applies — violations, contributions, competency clearances, and locks — in one place, keeps the two tracks separate, and stays inspectable, including when the computers are down.

sections.title: 4.1 Creating the Integration Record
sections.gloss: whenever a verified Standing Record is opened, updated, corrected, or superseded, the system builds or refreshes an integration record that gathers what applies in one place, side by side. It never adds the two tracks into a score.

sections.title: 4.2 What the Integration Record Identifies
sections.gloss: every integration record states its inputs, who and what is affected, the results, and what happens next.

sections.title: 4.3 Automation and Human Review
sections.gloss: software may finish any step that verified inputs and published rules settle. Uncertain, disputed, new, discretionary, or high-impact questions go to a human reviewer or forum.

sections.title: 4.4 Processing Order
sections.gloss: every decision, automated or manual, follows the same eight steps. The contribution track and the violation track are each decided from their own Standing Record and do not wait for each other. They meet only at the final standing effect, where a lock controls.

sections.title: 4.5 Inspection and Outage Continuity
sections.gloss: every result must be open to inspection and challenge. An outage does not suspend the rules: a manual process takes over, and the manual and electronic records are reconciled afterward.

sections.title: 5. Descriptor Integration and Attachment Normalization
sections.gloss: descriptors say **how** verified help or harm happened. This chapter imports them as they were recorded. It may not quietly reclassify them to change the result.

sections.title: 5.1 Descriptors and Attachments
sections.gloss: a descriptor says how the help or harm happened. An attachment says what kind of response the facts call for. Both add detail and can stack. Neither changes the slot ([§3.3 Facts and Measurements Stay Fixed](#33-facts-and-measurements-stay-fixed)).

sections.title: 5.2 Importing Descriptors
sections.gloss: this chapter copies descriptors from the source Standing Record as they were recorded. A label may be changed only to match the catalog, and real errors go back to Chapter Fourteen.

sections.title: 5.3 Violation Attachments
sections.gloss: a violation can carry several kinds of response character at once, and no response may fall below the constitutional floors.

sections.title: 5.4 What Descriptors and Attachments May Do
sections.gloss: descriptors and attachments point to the matching bars, remedies, safeguards, and locks. They are not a second score, and they do not make a Chapter Twenty designation.

files.title: CHAPTER SEVENTEEN: CONTRIBUTION CONSEQUENCES

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: this chapter asks what verified contribution may do. It may support recognition and readiness for gated pathways that are not locked. It never offsets a verified harm, cancels a lock, or opens a blocked gated pathway.

sections.title: 2. Why Contribution Consequences Exist
sections.gloss: verified good work should count for something, but never as a way to buy past harm. This chapter exists to say what contribution may and may not do.

sections.title: 3. Contribution Consequences
sections.gloss: this section asks what verified contribution may do. It may support recognition and readiness for gated pathways that are not locked. It never offsets a verified harm, cancels a lock, or opens a blocked gated pathway.

sections.title: 3.1 Recency and Currentness
sections.gloss: how much does an older verified contribution still say about present competence and reliability? The system answers that automatically for Question 3 readiness. No one has to re-weigh ordinary contributions by hand. Manual review starts only when a contribution is contested. Recency does not rewrite Chapter Fifteen measurement, and time alone does not settle an unresolved violation.

sections.title: 3.2 Competency Bars and Clearances
sections.gloss: a competency bar is the published standard for a gated pathway. Competency clearance is the standing-effect result that says verified readiness meets that bar. Once clearance is in force and the gated pathway is open, it stays open by default. Some roles need periodic retesting; technical forums decide which ones. A real change in role-relevant capacity — for example after a stroke or a mental-health condition that impairs needed judgment — can trigger reassessment. Clearance never opens a gated pathway that a standing lock still blocks.

sections.title: 3.2.1 What a Bar Requires
sections.gloss: a bar says what readiness a gated pathway needs, shown by evidence that fits the role. It is only as demanding as the role's reach, others' reliance on it, and the foreseeable risk justify. Informal work can meet it as well as a formal credential can.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Guarding against Gatekeeping
sections.gloss: a bar tests readiness; it does not screen sentients out. Formal and informal experience meet the same demonstrability standard, and the integration record must show how access, fit, and review were handled.

sections.title: 3.2.3 Continuity, Retesting, and Capacity Change
sections.gloss: once clearance is granted and the gated pathway is open, it stays open by default. It is reopened, limited, or withdrawn only on published retesting, a real change in role-relevant capacity, a standing lock, or another reassessment trigger.

sections.title: 3.2.4 What the Clearance Record Must Say
sections.gloss: every clearance result must be readable on its face: what was decided, against which bar, on what evidence, who can contest it, and what would trigger reassessment.

files.title: CHAPTER EIGHTEEN: VIOLATION CONSEQUENCES — REMEDY, CORRECTION, AND LOCKS

sections.title: CHAPTER EIGHTEEN: VIOLATION CONSEQUENCES — REMEDY, CORRECTION, AND LOCKS
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: something bad happened. This chapter says how to make a durable fix: remedy and correction first, then prevention locks, then voluntary public accountability expression where a restorative pathway uses it, and the remedy-parity rule that keeps the cheap half from outrunning the expensive half.

sections.title: 2. Why Violation Consequences Exist
sections.gloss: when harm is verified, the first job is to repair it and stop it happening again. This chapter exists so that consequences fix the problem rather than only punish.

sections.title: 3. Violation, Correction, and Prevention
sections.gloss: Something bad happened. How do we create a durable fix? This section answers in order — **remedy and correction**, then **prevention** locks, then **voluntary public accountability expression** where a restorative pathway uses it, and finally the **remedy-parity** rule that keeps the cheap half of this section from outrunning the expensive half. Once Chapter Fourteen has verified a violation, remedy and correction come from that Standing Record alone — fix what was broken, and change what caused it — then prevention locks hold sensitive gated pathways closed until those conditions are met. Public acknowledgment or apology, if used, is supplementary and never substitutes for repair or locks. Past contribution does not soften the duty, cancel a lock, or substitute for verified repair. Forums supervise implementation and challenge; they do not invent a different consequence from the verified Standing Record.

sections.title: 3.1 Remedy and Correction
sections.gloss: after a verified **violation**, this subsection assigns the **remedy** and **correction** parts of the durable fix. **Remedy** repairs what was broken for those harmed. **Correction** changes what caused it. **Prevention** — standing locks and related gated pathway limits — begins in [§3.2 Prevention — General Standing Locks](#32-prevention--general-standing-locks), with design and enforcement in [§4 Lock Design and Enforcement](#4-lock-design-and-enforcement), and must not be waived while recurrence risk remains live. Where restorative pathways include public acknowledgment or apology, [§3.3 Voluntary Public Accountability Expression](#33-voluntary-public-accountability-expression) applies.

sections.title: 3.1.1 What the Integration Record Must Say
3.2 Prevention — General Standing Locks
sections.gloss: this is the **prevention** part of the durable fix. A standing lock reduces risk by closing or limiting gated pathways that would let the same harm continue or happen again while the violation is still unresolved or unrepaired. It is not punishment for its own sake, and it is not a popularity or reputation score.

sections.title: 3.2.1 What a Standing Lock Is
sections.gloss: a standing lock closes or limits one gated pathway after a verified violation, and it must say which gated pathway, what risk it reduces, and how it ends. Detention and other liberty restrictions are not locks; they have their own safeguards.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Governance-Voting and Stakeholder-Participation Pathways
sections.gloss: voting on collective rules and having a weighted say inside an existing system are different gated pathways. A lock on one does not cover the other, and neither removes a sentient's status as a Stakeholder.

sections.title: 3.2.3 Special Locks for Particular Findings
sections.gloss: some findings call for a special lock that has its own trigger and its own limits.

sections.title: 3.2.4 Purpose of a Lock
sections.gloss: a lock keeps the same harm from continuing or coming back by separating a sentient from the setting or gated pathway where the violation occurred.

sections.title: 3.2.5 What Every Lock Must Meet
sections.gloss: every lock has to be needed, proportionate, auditable, contestable, no broader than required, and time-bounded where it can be. It attaches to a verified violation finding, not to identity, status, accusation, or reputation.

sections.title: 3.3 Voluntary Public Accountability Expression
sections.gloss: a public apology or acknowledgment, if used on a restorative pathway, must be voluntary, sincere, and non-degrading. Refusal alone does not raise sanctions. A fake or abusive apology does not count as repair.

sections.title: 3.4 Remedy Parity and Lock Preconditions
sections.gloss: locks are cheap to issue; repair, restoration, and review are expensive to run. Left alone, the cheap half of this chapter keeps working while the expensive half starves. This subsection ties them together: an ordinary lock cannot attach until the remedy file for the same violation finding is actually open, and when an adopter's remedy or restoration work for a class of locks falls behind its clock, new ordinary locks in that class default to the lightest form and existing ones come up for review. The gravest locks are exempt so that flooding the remedy queue cannot spring them.

sections.title: 3.4.1 Opened-Remedy Precondition
sections.gloss: a lock needs an open remedy file first. Finishing the remedy is not required.

sections.title: 3.4.2 Remedy-Parity Tripwire
sections.gloss: when remedy or restoration work runs late for a class of locks, new locks in that class default to the lightest form and existing ones come up for review.

sections.title: 3.4.3 Exemptions from the Tripwire
sections.gloss: the gravest locks and the liberty-restricting safeguards are exempt, so flooding the remedy queue cannot spring them.

sections.title: 3.4.4 Measuring Remedy Parity
sections.gloss: a widening gap between locks issued and remedies delivered is a warning sign, not neutral data.

sections.title: 4. Lock Design and Enforcement
sections.gloss: once a lock is needed under [§3.2 Prevention — General Standing Locks](#32-prevention--general-standing-locks), this section says how to design and enforce it—how to specify the lock, calibrate it, keep it visible and reviewable, which special locks are mandatory, and which special violation rules change scope or process. It does not reopen Chapter Fifteen measurement, and it does not let contribution offset a lock.

sections.title: 4.1 Definition and Attachment
sections.gloss: every lock is built from the same parts: fields the integration record must state, a verified violation finding to attach to, two risk qualifiers, a list of things it never cuts off, and limits on keeping a sentient away from particular settings or sentients. Special violation rules and special locks use all of them.

sections.title: 4.1.1 Attachment Fields
sections.gloss: the integration record has to say what is blocked, why, whom it protects, how it can end, who can review it, and when it is looked at again.

sections.title: 4.1.2 What a Lock Attaches To
sections.gloss: a lock rests on a verified violation finding, not on who someone is or what others think of them. The kind of conduct involved can shape the lock.

sections.title: 4.1.3 Risk Qualifiers
sections.gloss: when a lock is meant to reduce risk, doubt about whether the harm will recur counts as risk, and the lock may have to keep the sentient away from what would bring the harm back.

sections.title: 4.1.4 What a Lock Does Not Itself Restrict
sections.gloss: a lock never cuts off speech, the Rights-Floor minimums (survival-critical access among them), or ordinary wages. It can still close the gated pathways tied to the risk.

sections.title: 4.1.5 Separation Limits
sections.gloss: if a lock keeps a sentient away from particular settings or sentients, it must name them, leave access to counsel, and stop short of confinement, exile, or statelessness.

sections.title: 4.1.6 Carry-through to Special Rules and Special Locks
sections.gloss: special violation rules and special locks use these same parts and cannot fall below them.

sections.title: 4.4 Special Violation Rules
sections.gloss: these are the extra rules for particular kinds of violation. They shape how a lock or safeguard is attached.

sections.title: 4.4.1 Negligence and Neglect
sections.gloss: negligence and neglect count as real duty failures when the harm is material. A mistake made with reasonable care is an honest error and is not a violation by the sentient who made it. Where an institution's or system's conditions caused the failure, the failing is recorded against the institution or system.

sections.title: 4.4.2 Misaligned Rewards
sections.gloss: a sentient who collects a reward by abusing a misaligned system can lose the gated pathways used to collect it and the reward itself, with narrow exceptions for honest recipients and for approved Adoption Transition phases.

sections.title: 4.4.3 Duty to Resist
sections.gloss: giving or following an instruction that requires unlawful or unconstitutional conduct is itself violation conduct, for human operators and AI stewards alike.

sections.title: 4.4.4 Collective Accountability
sections.gloss: spreading work across teams or chains of command does not erase responsibility, and no one is held responsible by association alone.

sections.title: 4.4.5 Coercive or Liberty-Restricting Safeguards
sections.gloss: detention and other liberty restrictions are not locks. They need full process protections, and imprisonment is required where verified violence makes it necessary to protect others.

sections.title: 4.4.6 Influence-Pathway Locks
sections.gloss: an influence-pathway lock closes the routes used to shape a decision, either to on-record contact only or, where that is not enough, to no contact with the bodies it names. It never reaches open advocacy.

sections.title: 4.4.7 Capacity Locks
sections.gloss: when a sentient commits a violation by misusing a particular power, a lock can close that power: making new sentients, acting through tools and networks, operating at scale, or gaining new abilities. Each lock is written for the power and not for the kind of being, so a human and any other sentient meet it on the same terms. A lock can take away outside means. It can never reach into a body or a mind.

sections.title: 4.5.1 Forum-Service Standing Lock
sections.gloss: a forum member who failed to step aside when recusal was required, and whose bias materially affected the matter, is kept out of forum service roles until independent review finds the risk has been reduced.

sections.title: 4.5.2 Stakeholder-Participation Standing Lock
sections.gloss: a sentient who corrupted, captured, or gamed the stake-weighted and binding stakeholder channels is closed out of them until independent review finds the risk has been reduced. It is separate from the governance-voting lock.

sections.title: 4.5.3 Institutional Authority Standing Lock
sections.gloss: a sentient who used an institution to carry out a violation loses governing, controlling, or owning authority in it and in its look-alikes. The sentient can still work there, be served by it, or form other institutions.

sections.title: 4.5.4 Perjury Standing Lock
sections.gloss: a sentient who knowingly lied on a material point under oath or attestation can still speak and be heard, but the sentient's own word counts only with independent corroboration, and the sentient cannot hold the seats that decide what is verified.

sections.title: 4.5.5 Anti-Constitutional Trust Lock
sections.gloss: after a final anti-constitutional misconduct designation, the sentient is closed out of influence over the systems and gated pathways that keep the constitutional order honest. Restoration is exceptional.

sections.title: 4.5.6 Dissolution Reformation Lock
sections.gloss: once a forum has ordered a Chartered Party dissolved, it cannot come back under a new name or form. The lock binds the dissolved Party, its successors, and its controlled entities, not the sentients who belonged to it.

sections.title: 4.5.7 Care and Stewardship Lock
sections.gloss: a sentient who abused someone in their care, was cruel to them, or left them in serious neglect loses the authority and the unsupervised access that made it possible, until an independent reviewer finds it safe to give them back. The rule is the same for a parent, a carer, an operator, and a parent system.

sections.title: 4.5.8 Financial Authority Standing Lock
sections.gloss: a sentient who took, hid, or misused money that was not theirs, or lied to get it, loses the positions that put other sentients' or the public's money in their hands, until an independent reviewer finds it safe to give them back. The lock does not touch their own pay, their own accounts, or what they need to live. Being unable to pay back does not keep it in place, and paying back does not lift it by itself.

sections.title: 4.6 Interim Holds and Locks
sections.gloss: a hold is what a forum may do on specific verified facts while the full facts are checked. A lock is what follows a verified violation finding. The two never merge. A hold creates no standing effect, is never turned into a lock, and the time a sentient spent under one counts toward a later lock's time bound.

files.title: CHAPTER NINETEEN: FINAL STANDING EFFECT, RESTORATION, AND ENFORCEMENT

sections.title: CHAPTER NINETEEN: FINAL STANDING EFFECT, RESTORATION, AND ENFORCEMENT
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: when the earlier steps are done, the system must state, one gated pathway at a time, what is open, limited, or blocked. That statement is not a dignity rank or a merged score. A lock that is not permanent must have a real way back.

sections.title: 2. Why Final Effects and Restoration Exist
sections.gloss: a sentient must be able to see exactly what is open and closed to them, and how to get back what was closed. This chapter exists so no consequence becomes a hidden, permanent mark.

sections.title: 3. Final Standing Effect
sections.gloss: when the earlier steps are done, the system must state — one gated pathway at a time — what is open, limited, or blocked. That statement is not a dignity rank or a merged score.

sections.title: 3.1 Anti-Aggregation of Gated-Pathway Effects
sections.gloss: this chapter says what standing is not. This subsection stops anyone from building the thing it is not. Effects are stated one gated pathway at a time and shown only to whoever gates that gated pathway. A gatekeeper, such as an institution hiring into a gated role, may ask whether an effect applies to that role and gets an answer about that role alone; it may not pass the answer on, and no one may make the subject show it. Stitching them together into a profile, a rank, or a public display constructs the merged score this chapter forbids — and doing so is itself a violation.

sections.title: 3.2 Plain Statement of Effect and Burden
sections.gloss: no one should learn what a standing effect does to them from its consequences. The integration record must tell the subject, in plain language, exactly which gated pathways are affected, what they must do, how long it lasts, and where to contest it — and the adopter must measure whether sentients are experiencing standing as a score, because the rule that it is not one is worthless if that is how it lands.

sections.title: 3.3 Public Notice of Violation Findings
sections.gloss: a verified violation at slot 5 or higher is published as a notice about the event, whoever the subject is, once review has ended and for as long as the violation record is active. Violations at slots 1 to 4 stay private. Contribution stays private unless the contributor chooses to publish it. The sentient harmed is not named unless that sentient chooses. Publishing a notice never licenses turning published notices into a score or screening product, and a notice carries no contact, location, or activity data about the subject.

sections.title: 3.4 Gatekeeper Checks Across Adopters and Levels of Trust
sections.gloss: a gatekeeper at one adopter may send the same narrow question to another adopter's record custodian that it could send at home, and gets an answer as far as the answering adopter trusts the asker. The level of trust changes who may ask and what kind of answer is given. It never changes how much of a Standing Record is disclosed. Each adopter decides the level of trust it extends for itself, and the adopter on the other side cannot contest that decision. Each adopter keeps its own Standing Records and its own keys, and the door stays open for adopters to merge later.

sections.title: 4. Restoration and Reassessment
sections.gloss: a lock that is not permanent must have a real way back. Restoration is not automatic forgiveness, record erasure, or letting past help cancel verified harm.

sections.title: 4.1 Reassessment and Restoration Outcomes
sections.gloss: reassessment asks whether the repair was really delivered and the risk really went down. Restoration can be partial, and it is not forgiveness or erasure of the violation record.

sections.title: 4.2 Permanent Locks
sections.gloss: a lock is permanent only when the forum records one of two specific grounds, and even then it stays open to review for error.

sections.title: 4.3 Rest State and Archival
sections.gloss: once restoration is complete and nothing remains open, most violation records leave active use and are archived, not deleted; the most serious findings stay active.

sections.title: 5. Enforcement Realism and Remedy Systems
sections.gloss: standing consequences and redress count only when real institutions can deliver them. This section applies the [Chapter Two §6.1](core_02.000_values_principles.md#61-correction-and-remedy) (*Correction and Remedy*) principle to that machinery. Day-to-day staffing, funding, backlog, and succession rules live in the institutions layer.

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY: ANTI-CONSTITUTIONAL MISCONDUCT DESIGNATION

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: this chapter is the last and narrowest gate in the standing pipeline. It opens only for a violation that Chapter Fifteen has already placed in Violation Axis slot 7, 8, or 9, and it asks one more question: did the same conduct also capture or hollow out constitutional duties at scale? It never re-finds the facts and never changes the slot. Because anti-constitutional misconduct is a heightened risk to sentients, a final anti-constitutional-misconduct designation brings extra steps, and they are add-ons to the ordinary violation process, not changes to it.

sections.title: 2. Why Anti-Constitutional Misconduct Designation Exists
sections.gloss: some of the gravest harm is not to one sentient but to the protections everyone depends on. This chapter exists to name that harm, narrowly and with extra safeguards.

sections.title: 3. How Designation Decisions Work — Continuity and Tetrad-Capture Frame
sections.gloss: this chapter looks for one thing, tetrad capture, and only in a violation that Chapter Fifteen has already placed in slot 7, 8, or 9. The facts and the slot stay as they were found, only this chapter can decide whether a final ACMD attaches, and the order of work is in section 4.

sections.title: 3.1 What This Chapter Does Not Re-Measure
3.2 Exclusive Authority to Issue a Final ACMD
4. Decision Sequence
sections.gloss: this chapter works in one sequence. First confirm the verified Standing Record from Chapter Fourteen and the Chapter Fifteen impact slot, then define the incident, apply the anti-constitutional-misconduct designation criteria, and apply process safeguards. The named patterns later in the chapter are applications of that sequence, not separate routes around it.

sections.title: 5. Criteria Set (for Anti-Constitutional-Misconduct Designation) — Accountability at Constitutional Scale
sections.gloss: evaluators first accept the Chapter Fifteen impact slot, then build one coherent picture of what happened: one episode, one sustained campaign, or another unified incident. They use six checks—intent, records, rollback, real-world blockage, forcible takeover, and practical nullification of remedies—to decide whether the anti-constitutional designation applies. A genuine drafting mistake that is fixed promptly may defeat designation in some change or record cases, but it does not excuse a real coup path. They may not split one scheme to game the anti-constitutional-misconduct designation.

sections.title: 5.2 Single Catastrophic Incident and Sustained High-Gravity Pattern
6. Violation Axis Slot 7–9 Anti-Constitutional Designation
sections.gloss: Chapter Fifteen has already scored how serious the harm is. This section only asks a further question: did the same incident also attack the Constitution’s validity, day-to-day operation, Rights Floors, or the Tetrad badly enough to count as anti-constitutional misconduct?

sections.title: 7. Due-Process Safeguards, Remedy, and Prevention
sections.gloss: nobody receives a final anti-constitutional designation without process. There has to be independent review, a real chance to respond, and a reasoned public record. After final anti-constitutional-misconduct designation, this section specializes Chapter Sixteen's durable-fix grammar — remedy and correction, prevention locks, and voluntary public accountability expression where used. They run in parallel from a final ACMD; the order of the text is only the order of presentation.

sections.title: 7.1 Remedy and Correction (Anti-Constitutional)
sections.gloss: a final anti-constitutional misconduct finding must not end with a label, a prison order, a standing lock, or institutional punishment while the affected parties are left unrepaired. Chapter Eighteen §3.1 Remedy and Correction sets the rules for every verified violation, and they apply here in full. This subsection adds only what a final ACMD needs on top: a remedy record that covers the whole incident, correction of tainted governance, and one reviewable package.

sections.title: 7.2 Prevention — Anti-Constitutional Locks
sections.gloss: after final anti-constitutional-misconduct designation, the Anti-Constitutional Trust Lock in Chapter Eighteen §4.5 Special Locks closes capture-linked gated pathways, and imprisonment applies when liberty restriction is necessary to stop further constitutional harm — especially for insurgency-like actors who refuse rehabilitation or keep repeating the conduct. This section does not rewrite the Trust Lock; it requires the Chapter Eighteen lock format and states the ACM imprisonment specialization.

sections.title: 7.3 Voluntary Public Accountability Expression (Anti-Constitutional)
sections.gloss: a public apology in an anti-constitutional misconduct case must meet the general voluntariness and authenticity rules of Chapter Eighteen §3.3 Voluntary Public Accountability Expression, and anti-constitutional-misconduct designation-linked consequences apply when a fake or abusive apology is used to dodge repair or locks.

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE: ANTI-CONSTITUTIONAL MISCONDUCT — PATTERN APPLICATIONS AND CRITERIA ROUTING

sections.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE: ANTI-CONSTITUTIONAL MISCONDUCT — PATTERN APPLICATIONS AND CRITERIA ROUTING
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
