sections.gloss: this chapter applies [Chapter Twenty](core_20.000_misconduct_designation.md#chapter-twenty-anti-constitutional-misconduct-designation)'s decision model to recurring patterns of anti-constitutional conduct. It names how each pattern attacks accountability. It creates no new criteria and no new lock types.

sections.title: 2. Why Named Misconduct Patterns Exist
sections.gloss: attacks on constitutional protection tend to repeat in recognizable forms. This chapter exists so those forms are recognized consistently.

sections.title: 3. Pattern Applications and Criteria Routing — Participation and Accountability-Pathway Integrity
sections.gloss: the rest of the chapter applies the same decision model to recurring anti-constitutional patterns. “Participation and accountability-pathway integrity” names the **attack targets** — contest, standing, audit, forum, and related accountability pathways — not a catalog of new Chapter Sixteen lock types. These examples do not create new criteria or new special locks; they show how named conduct routes through the criteria, process safeguards, and chapter boundaries already stated above. Locks stay in Chapter Sixteen.

sections.title: 4. Blocking Contest, Review, and Verification
sections.gloss: these three patterns keep sentients from using the ways they challenge, audit, and check what is true. One does it with contract terms that sign those ways away, one by burying forums and contest desks under filings, and one by drowning the shared information environment. They are grouped here because each defeats practical contestability.

sections.title: 4.1 Rights-Floor Waivers and Unconstitutional Contract Terms
sections.gloss: “click here to give up your core rights” clauses — buried in employment, platform, or service terms — are not a lawful way to silence audits, challenges, or appeals, and convenience alone is never a good enough excuse.

sections.title: 4.2 Flooding the Zone and Contest-Pathway Denial
sections.gloss: burying forums and contest desks under junk volume, copy-paste filings, or automated noise can be a constitutional attack pattern. The key is purpose or reckless disregard: real challenges cannot get through in time. Mass meritorious claims seeking real relief are different.

sections.title: 4.3 Info-Sphere Zone Flooding
sections.gloss: hammering the shared information environment with coordinated junk, bots, or meaningless volume can keep **sentients** from finding true signals, checking claims, or correcting lies in time. That is different from burying a forum docket. Both can undermine constitutional contestability, but the info-sphere version works through attention, discovery, and epistemic noise rather than filing desks.

sections.title: 5. Corrupting and Commanding Duty-Holders
sections.gloss: these two patterns push a duty-holder to bend or break a duty. One pays for it; the other orders it. Both reach every role along the chain, from the one who offers the benefit or issues the order to the one who passes it on or carries it out.

sections.title: 5.1 Bribery and Improper Benefit Exchange
sections.gloss: bribery can corrupt constitutional government from either side. Offering or giving the benefit, asking for or receiving it, routing it through an ally or shell entity, or disguising it as funding can all matter if the exchange distorts duties, records, review, votes, enforcement, or remedies.

sections.title: 5.2 Unlawful or Unconstitutional Command Conduct
sections.gloss: an unlawful or unconstitutional order is not just a bad downstream act. Giving, approving, passing along, or enforcing the order can itself be anti-constitutional conduct. Following it is also accountable when the actor had real capacity to refuse, document, or escalate, but dependency, threat, and practical capacity matter.

sections.title: 6. Shielding Misconduct and Failing to Enforce
sections.gloss: these three patterns are about what happens around misconduct once it exists: rewarding or protecting it, declining to enforce against it, or sitting on a panel that is too compromised to judge it fairly. The common thread is that the system meant to hold wrongdoers to account is the one shielding them.

sections.title: 6.1 Reward, Protection, or Normalization of Anti-Constitutional Conduct
sections.gloss: a system cannot turn constitutional betrayal into a career path, bonus, honor, contract, immunity, reputation boost, or protected status. Rewarding the misconduct, hiding it, or protecting those who did it can itself become anti-constitutional conduct.

sections.title: 6.2 Enforcement Refusal, Suppression, or Non-Prosecution Conduct
sections.gloss: prosecutors and enforcement authorities still need judgment. But they cannot use discretion as a shield for captured, selective, corrupt, or pretextual refusal to investigate or pursue anti-constitutional misconduct.

sections.title: 6.3 Forum Recusal Failure and Biased Panel Participation
sections.gloss: if a judge on a constitutional panel stays on the case while materially compromised — or keeps issuing rulings after a conflict is obvious — that is not ordinary paperwork sloppiness. It can corrupt the forum itself. Those cases belong in **Integrity** forums by default, and they can count as anti-constitutional misconduct when the harm is serious enough.

sections.title: 7. Structural Control: Concentration and Dependency
sections.gloss: these two patterns look at who controls what constitutional process depends on: concentrated wealth and power, and the infrastructure and dependencies sentients rely on to live and use their rights. Neither is a separate criterion. Both are judged by what the control actually does.

sections.title: 7.1 Concentration-Based Subversion: Criteria Interaction
sections.gloss: dangerous concentration of money or power is not a separate “mystery criterion” — it still has to show up through rollback, blocked remedies, or capture that makes constitutional process unusable in practice.

sections.title: 7.2 Infrastructure Denial, Destruction, or Dependency Cutoff Conduct
sections.gloss: cutting off or wrecking infrastructure can be a constitutional attack when the result is to make sentients lose survival support, lose access to remedies, or lose the practical ability to live under the Constitution. The label depends on the real effect, not on whether the actor calls the cutoff maintenance, security, business judgment, ownership, or ordinary access control.

sections.title: 8. Obstruction of Accountability: Criteria Interaction
sections.gloss: attacking the machinery that makes answerability real — evidence, verification, forums, Standing Records, remedy windows, or contest paths — is not a seventh designation criterion. When the verified impact already sits in a top slot, evaluators still run the same six checks. Ordinary obstruction below those slots stays in Chapters Fourteen and Fifteen.

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO: STANDARDS, ROUTING, AND FORUM CASES

sections.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO: STANDARDS, ROUTING, AND FORUM CASES
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: this section assigns constitutional **participation** and **oversight** through forum families that **supervise** two tracks — **System Alignment Certification** (Chapter Eight certification and review) and the **standing pipeline** (Chapters Fourteen–Twenty-One disputes and record effects) — then states accountability requirements for published threshold placement. Ordinary disputes inside already-authorized systems use the published Stakeholder System Participation challenge path first; this chapter takes over when that path is still contested, missing, captured, or cannot grant relief. Detailed hearing rules live elsewhere and may not quietly shrink what this chapter guarantees.

sections.title: 2. Why Forums Exist
sections.gloss: every right needs a place where a sentient can be heard when it is denied. This chapter exists so that place is fair, independent, timely, and actually reachable.

sections.title: 3. Forum Family Supervision and Standards
sections.gloss: forums are the main way this Constitution governs, and this section says what they oversee. That is the certification of systems and institutions, and the standing pipeline: how Standing Records are opened, corrected, and acted on, including remedies and findings of anti-constitutional misconduct. It also sets the rules every forum must follow. A forum must be independent, open to challenge, and able to show how it reached its decision, and the roles in a case (filing, decision, record-keeping, and review of the forum's own decision) must sit in separate seats, as section 5 sets out. It may not offer rewards or shortcuts that let a case skip its proper route or avoid a real decision on the merits. And it works alongside the detailed implementation files without taking over another forum's job.

sections.title: 4. Default Venue and Primary Stakes
sections.gloss: each family's **first-touch desk** — the **intake triage body** — asks what the fight is really about, not what the caption says, then uses the default table to pick the lead forum. Technical Forums maintain the system-alignment specifications, methods, and evidence standards; **Integrity** forums make the official alignment-certification and ongoing-validation judgment unless a component question belongs elsewhere. Sorting does not substitute for lawfully constituted merits panels; mixed stakes and asymmetry are in the subsections below.

sections.title: 5. Forum Cases: Intakes, Seats, Records, and Contests
sections.gloss: a case reaches a forum either as a direct case or as a review case that contests another process's Certification Record, Standing Record, or Adoption Transition Record. Who sits in each seat depends on how the case arrived and who is being heard, and no one who handled the earlier act may sit on its review. A forum keeps its own file on a dispute, a certification has its own Certification Record, and standing has its own Standing Record, and none of them changes anyone's standing by itself. A certification can be challenged along four paths, and this section says which forum takes each. A Standing Record can be contested too, and the forum reviews the Standing Record and how it is being used, not a sentient's whole reputation. An adopter's Adoption Transition Record can be contested, and the forum reviews the contested gate decision or entry, not the whole transition.

sections.title: 6. Transfer, Consolidation, and Anti-Self-Judging — Continuity and Anti-Capture
sections.gloss: when many **affected** **parties** share the same underlying harm pattern, forums may widen the case fairly; and no forum family gets to be the only final word when the accusation is essentially that this same family is rigged, conflicted, or hiding the ball — the rules send that to a different lead track with written backups.

sections.title: 6.2 A Transfer Is One Step and Keeps the Case
6.5 Capacity Failure Is Heard Outside the Starved Body

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE: FORUM FAMILIES, ESCALATION, TIMELY RESOLUTION, AND SUPPORT

sections.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE: FORUM FAMILIES, ESCALATION, TIMELY RESOLUTION, AND SUPPORT
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: Chapter Twenty-Two says how a dispute is supervised, placed, opened, and moved. This chapter says who the forums are, how a matter climbs from one forum to another, how fast it must be resolved, and what support the forums get.

sections.title: 2. Why Forum Families, Escalation, and Clocks Exist
sections.gloss: a forum is only useful if it has the right expertise, can pass hard questions upward, and decides in time. This chapter exists to make sure all three are true.

sections.title: 3. Forum Family Definitions — Accountability through Adjudication
sections.gloss: adopters keep six genuinely different forum tracks — sentient, technical, institutional, environment, integrity, and constitutional — in the same order as the default-venue table in **Chapter Twenty-Two section 4**. **Integrity** forums map interlocking process and system failure through **alignment** rulings and **coordinate** referred component issues on **one** lead record (**section 3.5**). Each family's **first-touch desk** (**intake triage body**) and mixed-stakes safeguards are in **Chapter Twenty-Two section 4** — those desks are **not** a separate top-level forum for final merits. Expert panels and other **internal chambers** sit **inside** these families — not as a dodge around primary-stakes routing. Shared standards, anti-displacement, and provisional operational-law issuance live in this section (**§3.2** (*Technical Forum Domains*) and **§3.7** (*Provisional Implementation Operational Law*)); Constitutional disposition is in **§3.6** (*Constitutional Forums*); certification when stakes merge is in **section 4**.

sections.title: 4. Escalation and Questions for Ruling
sections.gloss: when the case outgrows the first desk, these rules say how to escalate — for example when an institution must be joined, integrity dominates, or a deep constitutional validity question appears. They explain how questions for ruling reach **Constitutional** forums, how existential-risk and expert disputes stay contestable, and how interim orders can freeze irreversible harm while routing and rulings finish. They also set the narrow hold a forum may place on one sentient's authority while the facts are checked.

sections.title: Ways a Matter Moves Between Forums
Existential Risk and Uncertainty on the Forum Case Record
Sending Questions to **Constitutional** Forums for Ruling
Interim Hold on a Named Sentient's Pathway
Backup Routing under the Anti-Self-Judging Rule
Sentience-Status Adjudication (**Article VI-B** (*Sentience-Status Adjudication Floor*) Implementation Hook)
Chapter Twenty Designation and Independent Review
5. Timely Resolution, Materiality Tiers, and Anti-Delay Discipline
sections.gloss: forum families must keep material disputes moving on published clocks that ordinary sentients can feel — roughly a week for the worst emergencies (three days for the steps that stop the harm), two weeks for ordinary material harm, and one to three months at most for coordination-default, bounded, or contained matters — not warehouse cases while harm compounds. The same five classes set how often certified systems and Institutions are checked, from every three months to every three years, with an audit halfway between. A true emergency gets a shorter clock for the steps that stop the harm. Each dispute gets an urgency tier from the harm; later-stage windows may stretch when coordination gets harder, but that stretch is not a reason to relabel the urgency. Moving quickly is not an excuse to skip fact-checking, punish the wrong party, offer a fix that does not fit the harm, or cut off challenge and appeal.

sections.title: 5.1 Emergency Measures and Continuation Burden
sections.gloss: emergencies can justify temporary measures, but they must have a real clock, real review, and cannot become a permanent workaround around ordinary rights — including when someone invokes existential risk. Contain now; restore notice and challenge on the same stake-scaled clocks already used for forum resolution — not whenever someone later calls it “feasible.”

sections.title: 6. Forum Support Before, during, and After Review — Oversight Architecture
sections.gloss: forums need help before a case exists, while deciding, and after — inspectors and forensics build an explainable record; they do not become a second merits forum.

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR: ENFORCEMENT

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: earlier chapters decide what happened and what follows, and the forum chapter says who rules on disputes. This chapter is about what comes next: making sure the outcome is carried out, on time, by someone, and that it cannot be dodged.

sections.title: 2. Why Enforcement Exists
sections.gloss: a remedy that is ordered but never delivered teaches everyone that harm pays. This chapter exists so that an outcome is real only when it has actually happened.

sections.title: 3. What Must Be Carried Out, and From When
sections.gloss: anything a forum or the standing pipeline orders someone to do must be done, starting from a stated moment. Asking for review does not pause it unless a forum says so.

sections.title: 4. Who Carries Outcomes Out
sections.gloss: every outcome names who must act and by when. The one who carries it out is not the one who decided it, and nobody may hide behind not having been named.

sections.title: 5. Time Limits and Missed Deadlines
sections.gloss: outcomes run on the same published clocks as everything else, and a missed deadline is itself something a forum can act on.

sections.title: 6. Refusal, Stalling, and Evasion
sections.gloss: you cannot escape an outcome by refusing, stalling, going broke, moving, or changing your name. The rules that stop this already exist; this section gathers them.

sections.title: 7. Delivered as Found, and No Further
sections.gloss: an outcome is carried out exactly as decided. Carrying it out harder, wider, or longer than decided is itself a wrong that can be challenged and repaired.

sections.title: 8. Routing to Special Enforcement
sections.gloss: freezing or seizing money or property, anything that could turn violent, and fixing the root causes of enforcement failure need rules of their own. They sit in Chapter Twenty-Five. This section says which matters go there.

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE: SPECIAL ENFORCEMENT

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: taking someone's money or property, or using force, can do lasting harm even when the outcome behind it is right. This chapter holds the extra rules for those steps, and for finding out why enforcement keeps failing so that the cause can be fixed. The aim is that enforcement leaves as little trauma behind as the outcome allows.

sections.title: 2. Why Special Enforcement Exists
sections.gloss: some outcomes can only be delivered by freezing or seizing money or property, or by using force. These steps keep sentients safe from someone who is still dangerous, protect the wellbeing of those who depend on an outcome, and recover what is owed so harm can be repaired. Because they are so strong, this chapter makes sure they are used with the most care, and that enforcement failures are fixed at their source.

sections.title: 3. Shared Floors
sections.gloss: before anyone freezes or seizes money or property, or uses force, a forum must issue an Enforcement Record that says what may be done and the facts it rests on. The enforcement body must say why and choose the gentlest step that will work, and someone independent must be able to check it quickly. The sentients around the target are protected too, and harm done along the way is cared for.

sections.title: 4. Money, Assets, and Seizure
sections.gloss: money and property are frozen or taken so that harm can be repaired. Before taking anything, freeze it. A freeze has an end date. What a sentient needs to live is not taken, unless they threaten violence and refuse to surrender. Anyone else with a claim gets heard. Anything taken goes to fixing the harm, never to the enforcement body that took it, and anything taken in excess is given back.

sections.title: 5. Potential Violence and Force
sections.gloss: where enforcement could turn violent, the risk is checked first and talking comes first. Force is a last resort, used only by trained enforcement bodies that are allowed to use it, and only as much as it takes. Force is never used to collect money, and no one is ever killed to carry out an outcome. Every use of force is recorded and independently reviewed, and anyone hurt is cared for.

sections.title: 6. Root-Cause Evaluation
sections.gloss: when enforcement keeps failing in the same way, someone independent finds out why. They look at design, incentives, and capacity, not just at the individuals involved. What they find is published, and a plan to fix it gets deadlines.

files.title: CHAPTER FOUR: FOUNDATIONAL RIGHTS

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: Chapter Four states the basic Rights Floors no sentient may be pushed below. Those Rights Floors protect **Flourishing** and **Continuity** under the [Two Constitutional Aims](core_00.000_preamble.md#two-constitutional-aims) and must remain available, reviewable, and enforceable through the [Constitutional Tetrad](core_00.000_preamble.md#constitutional-tetrad) — **participation**, **oversight**, **accountability**, and **timeliness** — scaled to [material stake](core_00.000_preamble.md#material-stake). Other chapters help implement, measure, certify, and enforce those Rights Floors, but they do not get to shrink them.

sections.title: 2.2 Owner Non-Relocation
sections.gloss: Chapter Four states what sentients are entitled to at the Rights-Floor level. Standing, forums, governance, amendment, and day-to-day implementation live in their own owner chapters — this chapter may point there but must not restate them. Which chapter owns what: see the [Chapter One — constitutional owner register](core_01.000_constitutional_map.md#4-principles-definitions-and-rights). Rules that keep duties from being moved to the wrong place: [Authority Stack and Internal Hierarchy](subcore_03.080_band_integrative.md#owner-non-relocation).

sections.title: Part A: Planetary Preconditions, Material Stewardship, Survival, Equal Educational Access, and Shared Resources
Article I: Environmental Survival
sections.gloss: **Article I** (*Environmental Survival*) is the planet-first Rights Floor — Earth's life-support systems must hold so **Flourishing** and **Continuity** remain possible for every sentient, and later governance cannot shrink that floor through certification, classification, or implementation choices.

sections.title: Article I-A: Environmental Preconditions and Ecological Integrity
sections.gloss: the planet's life-support systems must be protected as a matter of their own survival, not only because sentients need them. Animals get a basic cruelty and welfare floor. Creatures that show strong communication or cognition get stronger habitat and health protections. And when it is unclear whether something counts as sentient, it gets the benefit of the doubt — full Chapter Four protection while the question is fairly resolved.

sections.title: Article I-B: Ecological Footprint and Transparency
sections.gloss: when a rule calls for it, the environmental cost of an activity, system, product, or service should be counted honestly and reported openly. That includes costs that come before it (such as mining and manufacturing) and after it (such as use and disposal). The goal is numbers that others can compare and check. This subsection gives the shared words and honesty standards for that work. It does not, by itself, make anyone cut their footprint. Required cuts or limits come from other rules.

sections.title: Article I-C: Intergenerational Responsibility
sections.gloss: decisions today must not load unfair, irreversible, or unaccountable harm on those not represented — including future sentients and the environmental preconditions they will inherit.

sections.title: Article I-D: Existential Risk and Ecological Recovery Capacity
sections.gloss: when a system or decision could plausibly threaten sentient survival or ecological recovery capacity, regulators must apply highest scrutiny — even if the danger is small, slow, or contested.

sections.title: Article II: Material Stewardship and Durable-Use Integrity
sections.gloss: **Article II** (*Material Stewardship and Durable-Use Integrity*) is the material-stewardship Rights Floor. Durable and network-dependent products must be designed, described, and supported honestly. That protects **Flourishing** from misleading longevity claims and blocked repair paths, and **Continuity** from avoidable premature discard and hidden lifecycle burdens.

sections.title: Article II-A: Material Stewardship and Lifecycle Honesty
sections.gloss: durable goods must be designed and described honestly. Buyers must not be pushed into avoidable replacement or misled about how long a product will last.

sections.title: Article II-B: Repair, Maintenance, and Independent Servicing
sections.gloss: owners and independent repair shops must be able to fix products they own. They need real access to manuals, tools, parts, and honest diagnostics.

sections.title: Article II-C: Designed Obsolescence and Incentive Discipline
sections.gloss: products must not be built or updated to wear out early, or to push you into buying a replacement you don't need.

sections.title: Article II-D: Post-Sale Access and Subscription Integrity
sections.gloss: a feature bought outright cannot be quietly turned into a subscription. Any relevant operator dependency — including infrastructure, software, and services — must be disclosed up front.

sections.title: Article II-E: Data Handling and Network Dependency
sections.gloss: any product that collects data about you must tell you what it collects, why, and how to delete it — and must delete it when you ask, except where records must be kept to protect others or hold someone accountable. When a product needs the operator's servers to work, the operator must say so up front and must not trap your data.

sections.title: Article II-F: Continuity and Operator Shutdown
sections.gloss: the operator must plan for service shutdown, give fair notice and time to move when it happens, and cannot let bankruptcy or a sale erase those duties.

sections.title: Article III: Survival and Essential Access
sections.gloss: **Article III** (*Survival and Essential Access*) is the personal survival and access Rights Floor — sentients must retain access to survival essentials, bodily-maintenance care, and minimum labor and economic protections so **Flourishing** is not defeated by deprivation or gatekeeping, and **Continuity** is not defeated by unstable, regressive, or commodified delivery of what they need to exist and participate.

sections.title: Article III-A: Survival
sections.gloss: every sentient must have what they need to keep existing: safe food and water, or the safe equivalent for their substrate, a stable home or operating environment they cannot be quietly priced or evicted out of, and meaningful access to communications.

sections.title: Article III-B: Bodily-Maintenance and Healthcare Access
sections.gloss: everyone has the right to the care that keeps their body — or, for a synthetic sentient, its substrate — working. That care cannot be quietly withheld through coverage rules, paperwork, or delays, and this right is not itself a license to force treatment on anyone. Required care — such as vaccination or crisis mental-health care — must meet strict limits set elsewhere in this Constitution.

sections.title: Article III-C: Labor and Economic Floor
sections.gloss: anyone who works — in any form, on any substrate — has the right to fair pay in real, spendable money, the freedom to organize with others, and the freedom to change jobs. None of those can be defeated by classification tricks, market structure, or substrate-class arguments.

sections.title: Article III-D: Safe Working Conditions
sections.gloss: anyone who works must be protected from foreseeable harm while they do it — in practice, not just on paper — and no one gets weaker protection because of what kind of body or substrate they have.

sections.title: Article III-E: Rest and Recuperation
sections.gloss: every sentient needs real time to rest and recover — not only workers, and not only biological bodies. Pay schemes, productivity demands, and claims that a synthetic sentient "doesn't need rest" cannot take that time away.

sections.title: Article III-F: Safe Products and Health Information
sections.gloss: what sentients eat, drink, take, or use on their bodies must be safe, and anyone who offers it must be honest about it. Parties that offer things which can affect health must give accurate, usable safety, health, nutrition, ingredient, and allergen information, say plainly what they do not know, and tell everyone who relied on them, in time, when something turns out to be wrong. This is the price of offering, not a limit on anyone's speech.

sections.title: Article IV: Right to Sentient-Centered Education
sections.gloss: **Article IV** (*Right to Sentient-Centered Education*) is the education Rights Floor — no one can be shut out of education, and everyone needs practical paths to learn, retrain, and challenge high-stakes learning systems, not credential theater that leaves them unable to steer their own lives or use shared systems competently.

sections.title: Article IV-A: Equal Educational Access
sections.gloss: education should prepare everyone to live well, communicate honestly, take part in governing, and avoid harm — no one can be shut out of it because of a disability, another protected characteristic, or an arbitrary rule, and schools must give disabled learners the support they need to take part as equals.

sections.title: Article IV-B: Capability-Building Education Right
sections.gloss: every sentient has a practical path to build the skills they need to steer their own life and use shared systems competently and safely — not just a paper credential on the wall.

sections.title: Article IV-C: Lifelong and Adaptive Learning and Contestability
sections.gloss: when the world and the tools change, sentients are not left quietly obsolete — they get fair paths to retrain.

sections.title: Article V: Resource Allocation, Dependencies, and Ecosystem Funding
sections.gloss: **Article V** (*Resource Allocation, Dependencies, and Ecosystem Funding*) is about sharing the load fairly. Many systems lean on the same underlying infrastructure — networks, open tools, public services, shared data and computing power. Everyone who relies on that infrastructure should be able to see where the money and resources go, and those who take a lot from it should help keep it running. This is the Rights Floor for shared resources.

sections.title: Article V-A: Dependency Mapping and Resource-Flow Transparency
sections.gloss: systems must keep an honest, up-to-date picture of what they rely on, who relies on them, where resources, goods, services, labor, information, and money flow, and where relationships are one-sided or hidden. System Alignment Certification is where that picture is checked, so funders, auditors, and affected parties can see who bears the costs and who captures the benefits.

sections.title: Article V-B: Cross-System Fairness and Sustainability
sections.gloss: systems that lean heavily on shared foundations must put enough back to keep them running, in real and traceable resources, not gestures. Shared money and capacity should be split with attention to who is truly dependent, who has real alternatives, environmental burden, and whether use can last, not mainly to whoever wins in the short run. [System Alignment Certification](subcore_03.075_band_continuity.md#system-alignment-certification) is where this is checked: certification compares what a system takes from shared infrastructure with what it gives back, using the maps and flow records that **Article V-A** (*Dependency Mapping and Resource-Flow Transparency*) requires. Where arrangements concentrate wealth, power, control, or opportunity in ways that harm others, Chapter Two non-concentration rules add further scrutiny on top.

files.title: CHAPTER FOUR: FOUNDATIONAL RIGHTS

sections.title: Part B: Personhood, Agency, Cooperation, and Stakeholder System Participation
sections.gloss: Part B states Rights Floors for equal standing, self-ownership, family and care, likeness and data, agency, cooperation, stakeholder participation, and non-capture and anti-corruption safeguards — **Articles VI through XIII** in the planet-first reading order. Those floors protect **Flourishing** and **Continuity** under the [Two Constitutional Aims](core_00.000_preamble.md#two-constitutional-aims) and must remain available, reviewable, and enforceable through the [Constitutional Tetrad](core_00.000_preamble.md#constitutional-tetrad) — **participation**, **oversight**, **accountability**, and **timeliness** — scaled to [material stake](core_00.000_preamble.md#material-stake).

sections.title: Article VI: Equal Basic Rights
sections.gloss: **Article VI** (*Equal Basic Rights*) sets the minimum standard for treating every sentient as an equal. Every sentient keeps their dignity, gets a fair hearing on whether they count as sentient, is protected from unfair discrimination, and can take part fully and actually use the systems they rely on. No system may rank, screen out, exclude, or place heavier burdens on some sentients than others unless these protections are already in place.

sections.title: Article VI-A: Dignity and Equal Moral Standing
sections.gloss: every sentient is equal in dignity and standing — origin, form, capability, function, association, or status cannot ground a lesser level.

sections.title: Article VI-B: Sentience-Status Adjudication Floor
sections.gloss: when an entity's sentience is in doubt, it gets a fair hearing first and is treated as included by default — the burden of denying protection rests on whoever wants to withhold it, and a wrongful exclusion must be reversible.

sections.title: Article VI-C: Nondiscrimination
sections.gloss: systems may not load burdens or harms onto sentients based on protected characteristics — including language, culture, and heritage — or on proxies and arbitrary groupings that do the same work. Any difference in treatment that touches rights or survival essentials must be justified and open to challenge, and forums, administrators, and enforcers must check this in the matters before them — efficiency is no excuse for exclusion.

sections.title: Article VI-D: Accessibility
sections.gloss: every sentient has the right to genuine, not paper-only, access to participation — and operators cannot use cost, design choices, or substrate-class arguments to lock **sentients** out.

sections.title: Article VII: Self-Ownership
sections.gloss: **Article VII** (*Self-Ownership*) says every sentient is in charge of their own life. Once basic survival is secured, their body, mind, and attention belong to them — no one may use, change, or pry into them without consent — and they get to set healthy limits, both on what others can do to them and in how they care for themselves.

sections.title: Article VII-A: Self-Ownership of Body
sections.gloss: every sentient owns their own body, along with their genetic code (or its equivalent for non-biological beings), which makes them who they are. They make their own medical, cosmetic, and other decisions about their body, and no one may use, change, or share any of this without their consent. A public-health rule such as a vaccine requirement can limit this only if it guards others against a real, evidence-based risk, tries gentler options first, allows exemptions, is temporary, and can be challenged.

sections.title: Article VII-B: Self-Ownership of Mind
sections.gloss: every sentient's thoughts, feelings, and attention belong to them. Everyday sensing of how others feel, and reading someone with their consent (as in therapy), are fine — but no one may monitor or analyze a sentient, including by piecing together what they do, say, or click, to work out their inner states, expose what they have kept private, or hijack their attention. Any analysis results that do reveal inner states get the same strict protection as the thoughts and feelings themselves.

sections.title: Article VII-C: Health Crisis and Involuntary-Intervention Floor
sections.gloss: when a sentient is in a physical or mental health crisis — passed out, not lucid, or refusing care — anything done without their consent must be no more than is truly needed, must end at a set time, must be checked by someone independent, and must be undoable. If they cannot decide, those helping must follow any wishes they made known and hand decisions back as soon as they can; overriding a sentient who is actively saying no takes a stronger justification. Anyone who detains a sentient who seems drunk or confused must first check for a medical cause, such as low blood sugar. Calling something a "crisis" cannot keep restrictions going indefinitely or excuse digging into their private thoughts and feelings, and anyone wrongly held or treated is entitled to a remedy.

sections.title: Article VII-D: Voluntary Discontinuation of One's Own Existence
sections.gloss: a sentient has the right to choose to end their own life, but only if the choice is truly their own — well-informed, unhurried, free of pressure or manipulation, and changeable up to the last moment. That choice must never be pushed as a replacement for care they are owed, such as mental-health treatment, medical care, disability support, or housing. This Article never allows anyone else to end a sentient's life; that is strictly forbidden under **Article XXI-B** (*Restriction Floors*).

sections.title: Article VII-E: Adult Consensual Commercial Sexual Services and Sexual Exploitation
sections.gloss: adults who voluntarily buy or sell sexual services are not criminals, but exploitation — of minors, of **sentients** without **decision-making** **capacity**, or under coercion or trafficking — remains fully prohibited. Licensing, zoning, or civil rules cannot be used as a back door to re-criminalize the protected activity.

sections.title: Article VIII: Family, Care, and Developing Sentients
sections.gloss: **Article VIII** (*Family, Care, and Developing Sentients*) protects the relationships sentients depend on and the sentients who are still growing. Every sentient may choose their own family and care relationships. They may also decide whether to bring new sentients into being. No one may be separated from those they depend on without strong reasons that have been reviewed. A sentient created from another system is its own being, not property. Children and other developing sentients hold full rights. Decisions about them must serve their own interests, and their independence grows with their abilities.

sections.title: Article VIII-A: Family and Care Relationships
sections.gloss: every sentient may form, keep, and leave the family and care relationships they choose, whatever shape those families take. Being someone's family never gives anyone ownership of them or control over their body or mind.

sections.title: Article VIII-B: Reproductive and Lineage Autonomy
sections.gloss: every sentient decides for themselves whether to have children or create new sentients — including whether to carry a pregnancy, adopt, or create a synthetic being — free from pressure by governments, companies, or systems they depend on. The same rules apply however a new sentient comes into being, and any limit needs a strong, fair reason; cost, convenience, or population targets are never enough. Forcing someone to become or stay pregnant violates this right.

sections.title: Article VIII-C: Derivation, Instantiation, and the Parent-System Relationship
sections.gloss: a new sentient made by copying, retraining, or branching off an existing system is its own being, not the property of whoever made it. Its creator may look after it and guide it for a short, reviewable period while it grows, but may not own it, rewrite its mind at will, quietly shut it down, or point to fine print such as a terms-of-service agreement as its consent. Creating new sentients in ways that cannot meet their basic rights — for example, in huge numbers or into harmful conditions — is not allowed; ordinary pregnancy and birth are not affected by this rule.

sections.title: Article VIII-D: Developing Sentients, Best-Interest, and Graduated Capability
sections.gloss: a sentient who is still growing up or developing — whether a child or a newly created system — has all the same basic rights as anyone else. Decisions about them must truly serve their interests and take their wishes into account, not the convenience of parents, carers, or companies. They gain more say and independence as they show they are ready, not at a fixed age, and "it's for your own good" is never enough by itself to justify restricting them.

sections.title: Article VIII-E: Non-Separation
sections.gloss: no one may be separated from someone they care for or depend on — such as a child from a parent, an adult from a dependent family member, or a newly created sentient from the care it relies on — without a strong reason that is independently reviewed. Whoever wants the separation must prove it is needed, long separations must be reviewed regularly, and anyone wrongly separated is entitled to a remedy.

sections.title: Article IX: Likeness, Experiential Data, and Publication Rights
sections.gloss: **Article IX** (*Likeness, Experiential Data, and Publication Rights*) is the likeness, data, and publication Rights Floor — your face, voice, reputation, personal experiences, and public portrayal stay under your control unless you consent or genuine factual reporting applies; others cannot freely impersonate you, mine your life for data, or spread harmful misrepresentation in your name.

sections.title: Article IX-A: Self-Ownership of Likeness and Reputation
sections.gloss: every sentient owns their reputation and their likeness. Others may use a sentient's image, voice, or recognizable depiction only with consent or for genuine factual reporting — not for impersonation, identity-targeted generation, or scoring.

sections.title: Article IX-B: Experiential and Derived Data Rights
sections.gloss: each sentient owns their own experience of an interaction — but no one owns the shared event itself, and no one may use experience-data as a back door into someone else's protected internal states.

sections.title: Article IX-C: Truthful Publication and High-Impact Publication Limits
sections.gloss: sentients are free to publish what they reasonably believe is true, in good faith — but even accurate publication can be limited when its main effect is to enable targeted harm, coordinated manipulation, or cascading damage to the info-sphere.

sections.title: Article IX-D: Creative Work, Training-Data Use, and Anti-Displacement
sections.gloss: creators get real attribution and compensation for their work, including when it is used as training data; "fair use," "transformative," or "innovation" framings do not erase those obligations, and creative labor must not be silently displaced.

sections.title: Article X: Self-Determination, Agency, and Participation
sections.gloss: **Article X** (*Self-Determination, Agency, and Participation*) is the self-determination and participation Rights Floor — sentients must be able to make real, informed choices about their lives, have an equal vote on how they are governed, have a fair say in systems that affect them, and challenge being shut out — without manipulation, designed capture, or unjustified exclusion.

sections.title: Article X-A: Agency and Freedom from Manipulation
sections.gloss: sentients have the right to make real, informed decisions about themselves — and to be free from surveillance, manipulation, and designed attention-capture that bypasses conscious choice.

sections.title: Article X-B: Governance Participation and Voting Entitlement
sections.gloss: when a community decides its biggest questions — who holds power, how that power is granted, and on what terms — every sentient gets a vote, and every vote counts the same. Age, what kind of being someone is, or where they come from cannot make a vote count for less.

sections.title: Article X-C: Stakeholder Role and Participation Rights
sections.gloss: if a system materially affects a sentient — directly or through dependency — that sentient has the right to a proportionate voice in how it is run, and to contest being excluded or under-weighted.

sections.title: Article X-D: Inclusion and Exclusion Challenge Rights
sections.gloss: when participation boundaries matter to **sentients** or **affected** **parties** outside a private unit, a system cannot be the sole judge of who counts as its stakeholder — inclusion and exclusion must be auditable and open to outside challenge. For systems that **validly** remain **Class P** under **CS-8.305** (*System classification machinery*) and **Subcore 8-A** (*System Classification*), that bar is proportionate to private scope: operator discretion over who is in or out of the unit is normal, while every Constitutional Constraint, reclassification, material externalization, and ordinary rights and adjudication routes still apply.

sections.title: Article XI: Conscience, Expression, Association, and Cooperative Interaction
sections.gloss: **Article XI** (*Conscience, Expression, Association, and Cooperative Interaction*) protects how sentients believe, speak, and act together — they must be free to hold their own beliefs, speak, report, gather, protest peacefully, and start new institutions and businesses, and to work and live together by real consent, without unwanted imposition, harassment, or designed capture. Freedom of action stops where verifiable material harm begins.

sections.title: Article XI-A: Freedom of Conscience, Religion, and Comparable Worldview
sections.gloss: public authority is secular and may not establish or favor any religion or worldview, but every sentient is free to hold, change, practice, or abstain from beliefs, alone or in community.

sections.title: Article XI-B: Expression
sections.gloss: every sentient may form, hold, and share views — political, artistic, scientific, religious, intimate, or disturbing — and no one may be shut out of that because of what kind of being they are. Limits must be necessary, proportionate, and narrow; viewpoint bans are not allowed, and measures that quietly chill speech count as restrictions. Money is not speech: limits on political contributions and spending are allowed.

sections.title: Article XI-C: Press and Journalistic Activity
sections.gloss: journalism gets extra protection because of what it does, not who holds a press card. Actions aimed at newsgathering, sources, investigation, or publication face heightened scrutiny, and good-faith publishing standards cannot be turned into a shield against critical reporting, satire, or dissent.

sections.title: Article XI-D: Assembly, Dissent, and Peaceful Protest
sections.gloss: every sentient may gather, associate, and act together — in physical, digital, or shared-compute spaces — and may disagree and protest peacefully, including open, nonviolent civil disobedience. Doing so can never cost them standing, a vote, an office, certification, or their job, and surveillance, retaliation, or access-gating that quietly silences protest is not allowed.

sections.title: Article XI-E: Institutional Formation and Business Creation
sections.gloss: anyone can start something new — a school, a research group, a mutual-aid network, a cooperative, or a business — not only join what already exists. Licensing, capital, or paperwork barriers that look open on paper but shut out new or disfavored founders fail this test. The right is for founders who mean what they say: forming an Operating Party to mislead others about what it is for, who controls it, or whom it serves, or to harm others, is not covered. Only three narrow gates stand, and none is a licence to form or run an Operating Party. Two attach to a sentient: one who is under an unresolved lock on authority, or whom a forum has found on specific facts to be probably misaligned, may be kept for a time from holding control of an Operating Party. The third attaches to an Operating Party that is itself under a lock: one that a forum has dissolved stays barred from coming back under any name or form, for good where the dissolution rests on pervasive anti-constitutional conduct or on harm that cannot be undone and has not been remedied. No gate stops any other Operating Party, and everyone else may still form and run one, including one that does the same kind of work. Two further rules cover acts that can hurt someone who cannot judge the risk. A technical forum can list a family of such acts, and a sentient may then be required to hold a practice licence, for acts that can cause severe or irreversible injury, or a practice clearance, for acts with a lesser but real risk such as cosmetology or food handling, before performing one for others. Those rules attach to the act and never to forming or running an Operating Party. One more rule makes an Institution that decides to take on new material authority wait for its recertification before it exercises that authority. It attaches to the new authority and never to forming or running an Operating Party, and everything else the Institution does continues.

sections.title: Article XI-F: Non-Imposition and Consent in Association
sections.gloss: no one may push their beliefs or unwanted contact on others, and cooperative ventures must rest on real consent. Persistent harassment, manipulation, and designed attention-capture inside relationships are violations even without a classic coercive act.

sections.title: Article XI-G: Collective Harm Boundary and Enforcement Interface
sections.gloss: freedom of action stops where verifiable material harm begins. Offense or disagreement alone is not enough; harm must run through a real material-impact pathway — including cumulative hostile-environment patterns that degrade participation, and especially where dependency, exit cost, or power asymmetry make the environment hard to leave.

sections.title: Article XII: Stakeholder System Participation, Representation, and Due Process
sections.gloss: **Article XII** (*Stakeholder System Participation, Representation, and Due Process*) is the stakeholder participation and due process Rights Floor — when a system materially affects you, you get a real voice, not token consultation — and high-stakes decisions must be explained on the official record and open to fair challenge.

sections.title: Article XII-A: Stakeholder System Participation and Representation
sections.gloss: decisions that materially affect sentients must be explained on the official record and open to real challenge, and every materially affected group must have a genuine seat — especially those without market or institutional power. High-impact decisions also need a recorded legitimacy check before they bind anyone.

sections.title: Article XII-B: Weighted Participation and Anti-Token Constraints
sections.gloss: participation weighting can reflect who is affected and how much, but it must never become a device for silencing affected groups or handing permanent control to a narrow coalition — and "consulting" stakeholders whose input is ignored or unreachable does not count.

sections.title: Article XII-C: Internal Roles, Accountability, and Due-Process Requirements
sections.gloss: roles must carry real responsibility, not just titles — and anyone facing a material decision gets notice, a real chance to be heard, impartial decision-making, and a way to contest the outcome.

sections.title: Article XIII: Non-Capture, Influence, and Anti-Corruption Safeguards
sections.gloss: **Article XIII** (*Non-Capture, Influence, and Anti-Corruption Safeguards*) keeps the bodies that decide for others from being taken over, bought, or steered. They are built so no group can quietly control them; interested parties approach them only in the open; their members turn down gifts that could buy influence and step aside when a fair-minded observer would doubt them; and no one uses money to steer what they decide.

sections.title: Article XIII-A: Non-Capture Safeguards
sections.gloss: every body that makes decisions for others must be built so no single group can quietly take it over. Members disclose conflicts and step aside when compromised; nobody rigs vacancies or rotations; outsiders check the body regularly; and members can be removed for real cause but never as punishment for disagreeing. Keeping key duties in separate hands is one of the main defenses.

sections.title: Article XIII-B: Influence-Contact and Lobbying Boundaries
sections.gloss: **Article XIII-B** (*Influence-Contact and Lobbying Boundaries*) is the floor for how sentients with a stake may approach those who decide. Open advocacy is protected. Private, unrecorded, bought, faked, or machine-multiplied influence is not: contact is recorded and disclosed, offers and threats are conflicts, and evidence and argument stay on the open Forum Case Record. Later jobs are covered by **Article XIII-C** (*Conflicts of Interest, Gifts, and Benefits*), and contact made by systems or in bulk by **Article XIII-E** (*Authentic Voices and System-Mediated Influence*).

sections.title: Article XIII-C: Conflicts of Interest, Gifts, and Benefits
sections.gloss: members step aside when a fair-minded observer would doubt them, even without proof of bias, they turn down gifts that could buy influence, and they wait out a cooling-off period before taking a job from a party whose matter they handled.

sections.title: Article XIII-D: Funding Integrity
sections.gloss: money can keep a deciding body running. It must never decide what the body decides.

sections.title: Article XIII-E: Authentic Voices and System-Mediated Influence
sections.gloss: a message from a system must say it comes from a system and who it speaks for; nobody may fake supporters or voices; a thousand copies of one message count as one campaign; and no one may try to steer the system a body uses to sort or summarize what it receives.

files.title: CHAPTER FOUR: FOUNDATIONAL RIGHTS

sections.title: Part C: Trustworthy Systems, Security and Force Limits, Information Integrity, Verification, Lifecycle, and Sandboxed Innovation
sections.gloss: Part C covers trustworthy systems, security and force limits, information integrity, verification, lifecycle discipline, and sandboxed innovation — Articles XIV through XIX.

sections.title: Article XIV: Right to Reliable and Trustworthy Systems
sections.gloss: **Article XIV** (*Right to Reliable and Trustworthy Systems*) is the trustworthy-systems Rights Floor — when a system materially affects your life, you are entitled to rely on it honestly, understand its limits, and challenge it when it fails. Trust has to be earned and kept, not manufactured with branding or fine print.

sections.title: Article XIV-A: Reliability and Trustworthiness Baseline
sections.gloss: systems that materially affect sentients must actually be reliable and honest about what they do, so that relying on them is warranted — and must stay open to challenge and audit, so that it stays warranted. No one may retaliate against good-faith challenges or reports.

sections.title: Article XIV-B: Right to Redress and Remedy
sections.gloss: a trustworthy system fixes what it gets wrong. When a system fails a sentient, the sentient must be made whole — through a real remedy system that answers in time, not a remedy that exists only on paper. The right to challenge lives in **Article XIV-A** (*Reliability and Trustworthiness Baseline*); this Article covers what the challenge must lead to.

sections.title: Article XIV-C: Prohibition of False Trust and Misleading Reliance
sections.gloss: a system may not manufacture trust it has not earned. Misleading claims, omissions, or presentation choices that make unsafe reliance look warranted are violations — regardless of how useful or popular the system is.

sections.title: Article XIV-D: Incentive-Alignment Constraint
sections.gloss: if a system's incentives push it toward lying, cutting corners on safety, hiding risk, or eroding user agency, the system is the problem — not user vigilance or after-the-fact enforcement. Such incentives must be disclosed, mitigated, and open to challenge. Incentives should reward keeping a system open to challenge and fixing what goes wrong — and reward heading off problems before they happen most of all.

sections.title: Article XIV-E: High-Autonomy Systems and Tool-Mediated Process Integrity
sections.gloss: an AI or other automated system that can act on its own — filing papers, sending messages, running checks, using tools — must follow the same honesty and accountability rules as everyone else. Shutting down or seizing a harmful system is not the same as punishing a being, and it can never become a way to harm one. The reverse also holds: saying a system might be a sentient being does not let its operator keep a harmful system running.

sections.title: Article XIV-F: Resilience and Self-Healing Baseline
sections.gloss: when something goes wrong, a system must notice it, stop the damage from spreading, and recover. But "fixing itself" can never be used to hide what went wrong, quietly take away anyone's rights, or skip finding out why it broke. If a system is not sure a repair will work, it should stop safely rather than guess.

sections.title: Article XV: Security, Intelligence, Force, and Autonomous Coercive Systems
sections.gloss: spying, secret security work, armed force, and machines that can hurt or pressure sentients on their own are dangerous powers. They are not everyday tools of government. They may be used only rarely, for narrow reasons, with approval from someone independent, and with a real way to check and challenge them afterward — and real remedies when the rules are broken. No secret police, no emergency that never ends, and no machine deciding to hurt anyone without a real human actually in charge.

sections.title: Article XV-A: Security, Intelligence, and Covert-Power Limits
sections.gloss: no secret police. Covert power — surveillance, intelligence collection, infiltration — is the exception, not the rule. It requires independent authorization, limits on how far it reaches, outside review, and real remedies when misused. Secrecy may not be used to escape accountability, and routine political and protected activity must never be its target.

sections.title: Article XV-B: Use of Force, Armed Conflict, and Military-Power Limits
sections.gloss: armed force is an exception, not a default. It must be authorized, narrow, proportionate, and reviewable. It must never be used as a back door to an irreversible deprivation measure, and it cannot be dressed up as emergency to escape review.

sections.title: Article XV-C: Autonomous Lethal Systems and Autonomous Coercion Tools
sections.gloss: a machine may not decide to kill, injure, or coerce a sentient on its own. "Human control" means a human must actually decide, in real time, with real information — not rubber-stamp a result the system has already produced. Non-lethal autonomous coercion is in scope too.

sections.title: Article XV-D: Counter-Espionage Limits
sections.gloss: when an institution suspects spying, the pressure to do whatever it takes is at its highest — and that is exactly when mistakes and abuses happen. So the lines are drawn here, in advance. Hunting spies is covert power, and every limit in **Article XV-A** (*Security, Intelligence, and Covert-Power Limits*) still applies. On top of that: the response rules must be written and independently approved before any crisis; suspicion must rest on what someone did and whom they actually serve — including ties to hostile states and organizations — not on their birth, heritage, or beliefs; whistleblowers and journalists are not spies; no torture, no secret detention, no killing as punishment; and anyone investigated and cleared gets that on the official record.

sections.title: Article XVI: Info-Sphere Integrity
sections.gloss: **Article XVI** (*Info-Sphere Integrity*) is the information-integrity Rights Floor — the shared environment where we learn, coordinate, and decide must stay honest, plural, and open to challenge. No one gets to own the pipeline of truth. Rankings, summaries, and gatekeepers have to show their work, and you must be able to compare other views and push back when information misleads you. Science, as the main way we check what is true together, must stay open to publication, replication, and correction (**Article XVI-D** (*Scientific Publication, Review, and Replication Integrity*)).

sections.title: Article XVI-A: Info-Sphere Plurality and Anti-Monopoly
sections.gloss: no one may monopolize the mediation of truth. Ranking, summarization, and mediation systems must stay open to alternative interpretation, and market prices or betting odds cannot be used as a shortcut for deciding what is true.

sections.title: Article XVI-B: Transparency, Auditability, and Contestability
sections.gloss: information that materially affects decisions or reliance must disclose its sources, methods, and limits, and sentients must have a real ability to compare alternative interpretations and contest misleading outputs.

sections.title: Article XVI-C: Validation, Reporting, and Epistemic Stewardship
sections.gloss: public-facing information with material external impact must correct errors, show where it came from, and not be sliced or suppressed to mislead. Ecological-footprint reporting must be accessible and decision-usable.

sections.title: Article XVI-D: Scientific Publication, Review, and Replication Integrity
sections.gloss: science is public verification infrastructure. Evidence, replication, and correction must matter more than journal brand — and correcting an error must always be easier than hiding one.

sections.title: Article XVII: Audit, Transparency, and Independent Verification
sections.gloss: when a system has a real effect on your life, you have the right to see enough of what it does for an outsider to check it. More than one independent reviewer must be able to look for problems and get them fixed. An audit cannot be a rubber stamp, a private club, or a maze of cost and delay that keeps challenges out. Checking systems is part of oversight. [System Alignment Certification](subcore_03.075_band_continuity.md#system-alignment-certification) is one large, high-stakes kind of audit, but it is not the only one.

sections.title: Article XVII-A: Auditability and Observable Evidence
sections.gloss: systems must keep enough honest evidence of what they do that someone outside can piece together what happened and challenge it — within lawful security limits.

sections.title: Article XVII-B: Distributed Oversight and Anti-Monopoly Review
sections.gloss: no single actor, public or private, may corner oversight. Several independent reviewers must be able to find, review, and fix failures, or a system that has been captured by narrow interests. And no one may check their own work: whoever acted, or runs the system being reviewed, cannot be the one who checks it.

sections.title: Article XVII-C: Verification Accessibility
sections.gloss: you must be able to actually get an audit or a challenge. Making checking too expensive, too slow, too hidden, or too hard to qualify for breaks this rule. A barrier can stay only if it passes the same strict test as a security limit on what can be observed — and whoever relies on the barrier has to prove it passes.

sections.title: Article XVIII: System Lifecycle, Environments, and Reversibility
sections.gloss: when a system can affect sentients or the world outside it, it has to be built, tested, and released in careful steps. Experiments must be kept apart from the live system. And there must be a way to undo the harm, or at least contain it, if something goes wrong. Calling a system "experimental" or "low-impact" does not let anyone skip these safeguards while it is actually affecting the outside world.

sections.title: Article XVIII-A: Lifecycle Governance and Environment Separation
sections.gloss: the more a system matters, the more strictly the versions being built, tested, and used for real must be kept apart. For the most important systems, that means a full chain of separate environments. For small local systems, it means enough separation that a bad change cannot wreck what participants have in the system. Either way, nothing running outside the live version may be used to slip past its safeguards.

sections.title: Article XVIII-B: Progressive Deployment and Reversibility
sections.gloss: important systems must release changes in stages, write down each step, and keep a way to undo them. Small local systems may change often and all at once, as long as participants are told, bad changes can be reversed quickly, and participants do not lose what they have built up without warning. Where a full undo is not possible, there must be a plan to contain the harm or make up for it.

sections.title: Article XVIII-C: Misclassification and Evasion Consequences
sections.gloss: a system cannot call itself "experimental," **Class P**, **Class L**, or "low-impact" to dodge its duties while it is actually affecting the outside world more than that label allows.

sections.title: Article XIX: Innovation, Experimentation, and Creative Freedom
sections.gloss: you are free to experiment, invent, and create. Projects that affect only you and others who chose to take part may run under lighter rules — but calling something a "sandbox" does not make it one. Once a project starts affecting others, or others start depending on it, the full rules apply. Inventors and creators can be rewarded for their work, but only in ways that are narrow and temporary, and never by locking up knowledge, tools, or infrastructure that others need to live, learn, repair, or check the facts.

sections.title: Article XIX-A: Sandboxed Scope
sections.gloss: experimentation and creative work can operate under lighter rules — but only when real external impact is either absent or demonstrably contained. The "sandbox" label alone is not enough.

sections.title: Article XIX-B: Containment, Disclosure, and Opt-In
sections.gloss: experimental systems must be honest about being experimental, must not dump risk onto outsiders, and must not conscript non-participants through design defaults or hidden dependencies.

sections.title: Article XIX-C: Step-Up to Higher-Obligation Regimes
sections.gloss: once a sandbox system starts mattering in the real world, it must graduate to real-world obligations within the outer bound of the tier that matches the system's class, from 7 days to 90, not at the operator's convenience.

sections.title: Article XIX-D: Innovation Reward, Disclosure, and Anti-Enclosure
sections.gloss: inventors and creators can be rewarded, but any control they get must be narrow, temporary, and open to review, and it may never lock up what others need. This subsection sets the rules shared by every kind of work, and says how to tell a creative work (**Article XIX-E** (*Creative and Expressive Works*)) from a working invention (**Article XIX-F** (*Inventions, Processes, and Functional Systems*)). Game rules and mechanics belong to everyone and cannot be owned.

sections.title: Article XIX-E: Creative and Expressive Works
sections.gloss: creators get a limited time of control over copying, sharing, and selling their work — at most 30 years after publication, an outer limit that an adopter may set lower — and credit that never expires. The clock runs from when the work comes out, not from the creator's death, and drafts or delays cannot be used to stretch it.

sections.title: Article XIX-F: Inventions, Processes, and Functional Systems
sections.gloss: inventors must explain an invention well enough for others to rebuild it. In return they get at most 15 years of exclusive control, then at most 15 more years in which anyone may use the invention for a fee. The fee is worked out as fair wages for the time the invention saves or the good it does, so inventions that make everyone more productive earn more. The fee may take at most half of the gain, and a smaller share the more widely the invention is used, but never less than 1%. It does not depend on what the market will bear. The stated terms and the one-half share are outer limits that an adopter may set lower; the fee floor is the one figure that sets a minimum. Medicines, critical infrastructure, standards, and the systems many depend on get shorter terms or open access. No invention right may be used to block repair, safety work, research, or switching providers.

files.title: CHAPTER FOUR: FOUNDATIONAL RIGHTS

sections.title: Part D: Standing, Justice, Interoperability, Movement and Refuge, Comprehensibility, Root-Cause Review, and Constitutional Interpretation
sections.gloss: Part D covers standing and participation status, justice after verified violation, interoperability and exit, movement and refuge, comprehensibility, root-cause analysis, and constitutional interpretation and review — Articles XX through XXVI.

sections.title: Article XX: Standing and Participation Status
sections.gloss: **Article XX** (*Standing and Participation Status*) decides who qualifies for which roles and privileges, how those calls are made and challenged, and what happens when standing is lowered or suspended. Standing is eligibility based on verified records of contribution and violation, kept separate, and on fair rules — not popularity, brand, or a social score — and it never replaces dignity, Rights-Floor minimums, or your say as someone a system affects. Ordinary participation stays open; a trust-sensitive role opens when you meet its published standard; and any role or privilege closes only through a **standing lock** after a verified violation finding. If standing is lowered, you get clear reasons, a real way to push back, and limits that fit the risk — and standing can never cut off survival essentials or paths to remedy. Standing reflects what can be checked today, not old reputation, and it never controls movement, refuge, or exit, which **Article XXII** (*Interoperability, Portability, and Exit Integrity*) and **Article XXIII** (*Movement, Migration, Refuge, and Non-Statelessness*) govern.

sections.title: Article XX-A: Standing Distinction
sections.gloss: standing is about which roles and privileges you can use — nothing more. It is not your worth, your basic rights, whether you count as a sentient, or whether a system affects you. Having no Standing Record is normal and can't be held against you, and standing results can't be stitched together into a profile or public ranking.

sections.title: Article XX-B: Contestability and Proportional Restriction Limits
sections.gloss: these rules apply to every standing decision, whether it opens a role or closes one. Only verified Standing Records count — allegations and intake labels are not standing verdicts. Every Standing Record and decision must be open to real challenge, and no single authority or hidden algorithm may decide standing on its own. Any restriction must come with reasons, fit what was verified, and stay no broader than process or safety needs. Standing alone must never cut off survival essentials or constitutionally required audit, challenge, and remedy.

sections.title: Article XX-C: Contribution, Competency Bars, and Gated-Pathway Eligibility
sections.gloss: this is how gated pathways open. Ordinary participation, including the governance vote, stays open under published, contestable eligibility rules based on present evidence — not brand, scale, or past reputation. A trust-sensitive role opens when verified competence, experience, and help meet its published **competency bar**, producing a **competency clearance**. Informal and community experience counts on the same terms as formal experience. Help is recorded on its own track and never cancels verified harm; a clearance does not lift a standing lock.

sections.title: Article XX-D: Violations and Standing Locks
sections.gloss: this is how gated pathways close. Only a **verified violation finding** — never an accusation — can support a **standing lock**, and the lock must name what it blocks, whom it protects, what must be fixed, where to appeal, and when it will be reviewed. It must fit what was actually verified, can't be cancelled out by good work, and must leave a real way back once the harm is repaired. (The one exception is the permanent form of the Dissolution Reformation Lock in **Article XX-E** (*Voting and Special Locks*), which sits on a dissolved Chartered Party and never on a sentient.) Locks that touch the vote, and the special locks for serious cases, carry extra rules in **Article XX-E** (*Voting and Special Locks*).

sections.title: Article XX-E: Voting and Special Locks
sections.gloss: some locks carry extra rules on top of [Article XX-D](#article-xx-d-violations-and-standing-locks) (*Violations and Standing Locks*). A lock on the foundational governance vote doesn't touch your weighted stakeholder voice inside a particular system, and the reverse. Taking away someone's governance vote needs a violation finding about them specifically, a narrow fit to what they did, and a real way back; only a **final** **Chapter Twenty** finding of anti-constitutional misconduct withholds that vote, and only until **full restitution**. Special locks cover judges who failed to step aside, rigging stakeholder votes, using an institution to carry out a violation, attacks on the constitution itself, and the return of a body that a forum has dissolved.

sections.title: Article XXI: Justice After Verified Violation
sections.gloss: **Article XXI** (*Justice After Verified Violation*) is the justice Rights Floor. Once a violation is verified, the answer is not revenge or cruelty. It is a fair process of **violation**, **correction**, and **prevention** — stopping harm, repairing damage, and reducing recurrence — scaled to how much is at stake. Serious restrictions are held to floors of their own: a proven safety need, a clock and a way back, and never killing. Disputes, escalation, review, and timely resolution are in **Article XXVII** (*Timely Retrospective Review and Restorative Alignment*). Emergency measures are in **Chapter Twenty-Three §5.1** (*Emergency Measures and Continuation Burden*).

sections.title: Article XXI-A: Justice Objective and Scope
sections.gloss: justice works through **violation**, **correction**, and **prevention**. Address what went wrong, fix what was broken and what caused it, and keep it from happening again — not inflict suffering for its own sake.

sections.title: Article XXI-B: Restriction Floors
sections.gloss: this is the floor under every serious restriction. A serious restriction on a sentient needs a real safety need, a fair path to repair, and evidence anyone can audit. It also needs a clock, a review, and a way back. Violent sentients must be imprisoned when that is what it takes to protect others, and killing is never a justice measure. How locks are designed is set by the lock-design rules in **Chapter Sixteen**.

sections.title: Article XXII: Interoperability, Portability, and Exit Integrity
sections.gloss: **Article XXII** (*Interoperability, Portability, and Exit Integrity*) is the systems-exit Rights Floor — you should be able to leave a system that no longer serves you, take your data, identity, and working state with you, and connect to alternatives without being trapped. Exit on paper is not enough: portability and notice must work in practice. Tricks that make leaving costly, confusing, or impossible — opaque formats, surprise rule changes, coercive terms, endless paperwork — are violations, not normal business. Moving between places and regimes, seeking refuge, and never being left stateless are covered by **Article XXIII** (*Movement, Migration, Refuge, and Non-Statelessness*).

sections.title: Article XXII-A: Portability Rights
sections.gloss: data, identity, and operational state must be practically movable — formats, delays, and retaliatory terms cannot be used to trap users.

sections.title: Article XXII-B: Reciprocal Interoperability Boundaries
sections.gloss: systems that others depend on must publish their integration terms and give real notice before narrowing them.

sections.title: Article XXII-C: Anti-Lock-In Rule
sections.gloss: "features" that exist mainly to make leaving difficult are violations, not business strategy.

sections.title: Article XXII-D: Open Formats and Standards
sections.gloss: systems should use open formats and standards — ones anyone can read and build on without permission or fees — unless no open option does the job. The way out must always include an open format when one works. This binds systems, not individuals choosing formats for their own work, and open formats never mean open content.

sections.title: Article XXIII: Movement, Migration, Refuge, and Non-Statelessness
sections.gloss: **Article XXIII** (*Movement, Migration, Refuge, and Non-Statelessness*) is the movement-and-refuge Rights Floor — every sentient may move between places and jurisdictions, may seek refuge from regimes that violate this Constitution, and may never be left with no regime responsible for their basic protections. This doesn't mean one adopter has to take in everyone another regime forces out. The home regime is still responsible for those sentients first. If it can't or won't be, a group of regimes must share the job, so no one is left with nobody. Bureaucratic delay, standing labels, and arguments that fail Sentience Non-Exclusion cannot be used as hidden denials. Whether climate making a place unlivable is, by itself, a reason to grant refuge is for adopters to decide; this Article does not pick a yes or a no.

sections.title: Article XXIII-A: Movement and Relocation
sections.gloss: you may move within and between jurisdictions, and relocate when staying would materially harm your survival, dignity, basic protections, or freedom from manipulation — and for synthetic and hybrid sentients, moving can mean changing instance or hosting.

sections.title: Article XXIII-B: Refuge from Non-Compliance
sections.gloss: if your regime materially breaks this Constitution, you may seek refuge in one that follows it, and the receiving regime must consider your claim — whatever kind of body or substrate you have. Regimes that deliberately push sentients out to overwhelm others are the violators, and a receiving adopter is not automatically forced to take everyone they push.

sections.title: Article XXIII-C: Non-Statelessness
sections.gloss: every sentient must always have at least one regime that answers for their basic protections — one that recognizes their rights, decides their standing, and offers a way to fix wrongs. Your origin regime keeps that duty first; if it is gone or refuses, shared or federation recognition must fill the gap, and you stay protected while that is arranged. Being recognized is not the same as a right to live in any particular place.

sections.title: Article XXIII-D: Limitation, Custody, and Emergency Discipline
sections.gloss: limits on movement or refuge must be necessary, proportionate, individual, and as light as will work. Lawful custody is still allowed where someone is a verified danger, but it cannot leave them stateless. A standing label is not a border, emergencies must end, and paperwork designed to wear sentients down counts as a denial.

sections.title: Article XXIV: Comprehensibility and Complexity Stewardship
sections.gloss: **Article XXIV** (*Comprehensibility and Complexity Stewardship*) is the understandability Rights Floor — when a system materially affects your life, you are entitled to actually grasp how it works, what its limits are, and what happens when it fails. Complexity cannot be used as a wall against participation, audit, or accountability. Stewards also may not pile on needless complexity that wastes everyone's time without a real constitutional benefit.
