sections.title: Article XXIV-A: Proportional Comprehensibility Right
sections.gloss: if a system materially affects **sentients**, operators, stakeholders, and oversight must actually be able to understand how it works and fails — not just specialists.

sections.title: Article XXIV-B: Complexity Audit and Modularity Requirements
sections.gloss: complexity cannot be used — technically, organizationally, contractually, or procedurally — as a wall against audit, contest, or correction.

sections.title: Article XXV: Root Cause Analysis and Adaptive Response
sections.gloss: **Article XXV** (*Root Cause Analysis and Adaptive Response*) is the find-the-real-problem-and-fix-it-right floor. When something breaks, degrades, or keeps failing, you are entitled to more than a press release or a band-aid. Systems must figure out what actually caused the harm — including causes that show up late or build up over time — address those causes where they can, and leave an official record others can check and challenge. Quick containment is allowed; permanent fixes without honest diagnosis are not.

sections.title: Article XXV-A: Diagnostic Rigor and Causal Attribution
sections.gloss: root-cause findings must be written down, open to challenge, and open to correction — not sealed behind authority.

sections.title: Article XXV-B: Auditability, Challenge, and Reversibility Preference
sections.gloss: when you are not sure, pick the fix you can walk back. Uncertainty cannot be used as a reason to freeze protection or to pretend permanent measures are certain.

sections.title: Article XXVI: Constitutional Interpretation, Review, and Anti-Capture Safeguards
sections.gloss: **Article XXVI** (*Constitutional Interpretation, Review, and Anti-Capture Safeguards*) is the who-gets-to-say-what-the-constitution-means floor. When constitutional questions arise, the answer must come from designated Constitutional Forums — not from whoever is loudest, most powerful, or most convenient for the institution. Their rulings have to be written down with real reasons, open to independent challenge, and protected against capture by any single bloc. They cannot expand their own power, shut down review, or use "restructuring" to punish dissent.

sections.title: Article XXVI-A: Bounded Interpretive Mandate and Public Reasons
sections.gloss: Constitutional Forums rule on constitutional questions, not on everything. They cannot quietly expand their own turf or shut down challenge pathways. Every binding ruling must be published in time to challenge, with real reasons and the evidence behind them.

sections.title: Article XXVI-B: Challenge Rights and Independent Review
sections.gloss: if a ruling affects you, you can ask a different body to look at it again — not the panel that made it. That reviewer can fix, pause, or undo the ruling if the Forum Case Record shows a serious mistake, capture, or a Rights-Floor violation.

sections.title: Article XXVI-C: Constitutional Forum Independence and External Review
sections.gloss: the general rules against capture in [**Article XIII-A** (*Non-Capture Safeguards*)](core_04.010_rights_part_b.md#article-xiii-a-non-capture-safeguards) apply to every decision-making body. **Constitutional Forums** — the bodies that decide what the Constitution means — are held to them at their strictest. Their outside checkups are mandatory and are not scaled down.

sections.title: Article XXVI-D: Removal for Cause and Non-Entrenchment
sections.gloss: **Constitutional Forum** panelists can be removed for real cause through due process, exactly as under [**Article XIII-A** (*Non-Capture Safeguards*)](core_04.010_rights_part_b.md#article-xiii-a-non-capture-safeguards). For the bodies that interpret the Constitution, the ban on using "removal," "restructuring," or "redesign" as a weapon against independence or dissent is applied with special force.

files.title: CHAPTER FOUR: FOUNDATIONAL RIGHTS

sections.title: Part E: Conflict Resolution, Review, Constitutional Evolution, and Adoption Transition
sections.gloss: Part E covers conflict resolution, review-and-resolution discipline, constitutional evolution, and Adoption Transition — Articles XXVII through XXIX, including re-baselining under **Article XXIX** (*Adoption Transition Governance, Continuity, and Re-Baselining*).

sections.title: Article XXVII: Timely Retrospective Review and Restorative Alignment
sections.gloss: **Article XXVII** (*Timely Retrospective Review and Restorative Alignment*) is the conflict-resolution and review Rights Floor, and the companion to **Article XXI** (*Justice After Verified Violation*). When sentients, systems, or institutions collide over constitutional Rights Floors, the answer is a fair, usable, contestable process — not indefinite delay or a permanent emergency. After emergencies or serious rights conflicts, systems must look back honestly, disclose what can be disclosed, resolve rights collisions on the Constitutional Collision Record, and keep restoration tied to real protection — on clocks that match what's at stake. [Timeliness](subcore_03.065_apex_timeliness_leg.md#timeliness-constitutional) binds each step: without it, the other duties hollow out while harm sits unresolved.

sections.title: Article XXVII-A: Retrospective Review and Disclosure
sections.gloss: after the emergency, look back honestly and publish what you find — with only narrow, time-limited confidentiality.

sections.title: Article XXVII-B: Rights-Collision Procedure and Restorative Alignment
sections.gloss: rights conflicts must be resolved on the Constitutional Collision Record; restoration is preferred where appropriate but must not replace real protection. Voluntary public apology rules are governed by **Chapter Eighteen** §3.3 (*Voluntary Public Accountability Expression*) generally, and by **Chapter Twenty** §7.3 (*Voluntary Public Accountability Expression (Anti-Constitutional)*) for verified anti-constitutional misconduct.

sections.title: Article XXVII-C: Timely Resolution and Anti-Delay Floor
sections.gloss: constitutional problem resolution is a coordination and restoration system — quick, efficient, and just — not a warehouse where harm sits for years. Material disputes must move on bounded clocks through intake, verification, standing measurement, integration, and remedy. Moving quickly is not an excuse to skip fact-checking, punish the wrong party, offer a fix that does not fit the harm, or cut off challenge and appeal.

sections.title: Article XXVIII: Constitutional Evolution and Non-Entrenchment
sections.gloss: **Article XXVIII** (*Constitutional Evolution and Non-Entrenchment*) is the no-permanent-lock-in floor for how we govern ourselves. Rules for who decides, how sentients participate, how votes are weighted, and how money flows must keep proving they still serve the Constitution — they cannot freeze in place just because they are old, familiar, or convenient for those already in power. When the Constitution itself evolves, that change must happen in the open, with stated reasons — not through emergency shortcuts or hidden implementation tricks. Review must speed up when capture, exclusion, or failure signals show up.

sections.title: Article XXVIII-A: Non-Entrenchment and Revisability
sections.gloss: governance must earn its continued authority through regular review — and must be reviewed faster when capture, exclusion, or failure is showing up.

sections.title: Article XXVIII-B: Periodic Revalidation and Transparent Change
sections.gloss: constitutional change must happen in the open, with stated reasons — not through emergency, implementation, or custody shortcuts.

sections.title: Article XXIX: Adoption Transition Governance, Continuity, and Re-Baselining
sections.gloss: **Article XXIX** (*Adoption Transition Governance, Continuity, and Re-Baselining*) is the moving-day floor. Nobody can run a full set of Rights Floors on day one, because a right is only as real as the forums, oversight, trained staff, and public habits that enforce it, and those have to be built. So when a community shifts from legacy systems to constitutional operation, this Article asks for two different things. What the adopter must **not do** — make things worse, start new violations, destroy possible minds, hide the gap — binds from the start. What it must **deliver** — access, review, remedy — becomes enforceable step by step, scope by scope, as the institutions and culture that enforce it are verified ready. The Rights Floors are the fixed target the whole way, and the gap to them is measured, published, and shrinking on a dated path. Temporary Adoption Transition powers are allowed when truly needed, but they must stay temporary. A Adoption Transition that is going well shows it: interim powers keep getting smaller, and the Constitution's normal institutions and processes — forums, standing and challenge paths, oversight, and ordinary governance — keep working better and carrying more of the load. A stalled or failed Adoption Transition cannot quietly become the new normal, and interim rules cannot be used to rewrite the Constitution by the back door. If things break down, there must be a lawful off-ramp and a traceable path to re-baseline — not indefinite limbo — and that reset is not trustworthy if the machinery meant to tell the truth about systems and conduct keeps rubber-stamping misalignment or misreading real harm.

sections.title: Article XXIX-A: Phased Adoption and Rights-Floor Continuity
sections.gloss: Adoption Transitions move forward by meeting real gates, not by clocks or pressure. What the adopter must not do binds from day one. What it must deliver becomes enforceable as the forums, oversight, capability, and culture to enforce it are verified ready — scope by scope, on a dated path. The gap, and the data showing it closing, are public.

sections.title: Article XXIX-B: Adoption Transition Authority Limits and Reauthorization
sections.gloss: temporary authority really is temporary — and an Adoption Transition that is going well shows it. You should see interim powers shrinking phase by phase while constitutional forums, rights processes, and ordinary governance machinery work better and take on more of the load, and the measured gap to the full Rights Floors getting smaller on schedule. Extending temporary authority requires real reasons and real data — and the longer it runs, the higher the bar.

sections.title: Article XXIX-C: Failure Off-Ramps, Re-Baselining, and Traceability
sections.gloss: when an Adoption Transition stalls or fails, there must be a real off-ramp — and a stalled state cannot quietly become the new normal. Resetting the plan is allowed, but only through lawful process, with reasons anyone can check — and never by lowering basic Rights Floors. A reset is not trustworthy if alignment certification keeps blessing misaligned systems or standing review keeps misreading real harm; fix that truth-telling machinery first, or governance is structurally unreliable no matter how polished the new plan looks.

sections.title: Article XXIX-D: Non-Compliant Property and Systems; Voluntary Turnover Incentives
sections.gloss: non-compliant systems and property can be remediated during Adoption Transition — but only through narrow, documented, reviewable processes that protect basic Rights Floors, bar pretext, and do not turn into retaliation or political targeting. Ownership also does not shield property that is being used to carry out anti-constitutional conduct, though that case runs through the anti-constitutional misconduct chapter, not through Adoption Transition powers. How institutions carry that out — roles, triggers, custody, appeals, funds, and incentive mechanics — lives in **CI-4.275 §1** (*non-compliant property, seizure, voluntary incentives*) through **CI-4.275 §3** (*operative Adoption Transition-scoped remediation requirements*).

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX: CONSTITUTIONAL CONTRACT, LEGITIMACY, AUTHORIZATION, AND STEWARDSHIP

sections.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX: CONSTITUTIONAL CONTRACT, LEGITIMACY, AUTHORIZATION, AND STEWARDSHIP
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: this chapter states the constitutional contract for governing power — what must be true for rule-making to count as legitimate and stewardship to count as constitutional. The minimum bar lives here; most operating detail lives in implementation layers.

sections.title: 2. Why the Constitutional Contract Exists
sections.gloss: power to make rules for others must be earned and kept, not simply held. This chapter exists to say what makes governing power legitimate.

sections.title: 3. Authorization and Legitimacy of Governing Authority
3.1 Mechanism Families, Auditability, and Pluralism
sections.gloss: whoever governs must show a clear, chosen rule for how power is authorized — elections, lotteries, federation votes, **treaty, compact, or Constitutional Charter** processes, or hybrids — not an informal shrug. The active rules must be visible and **open to verification**; silence, mere usage, or branding cannot count as consent. When authorization rots or is captured, **sentients** need real ways to challenge it and, where possible, to renew or replace power peacefully — and different legitimate arrangements may coexist if rights and non-domination hold.

sections.title: 3.2 Eligibility, Contested Selection, and Democratic Minimums
sections.gloss: you cannot bar someone from governing or critical stewardship roles with a birthday rule — fitness and readiness must be shown in ways that stand up to scrutiny, not smuggled in as age. A real legitimacy mechanism offers real choices, protects dissent enough that it can matter, and includes a credible path to hand power over — not a rigged contest, not retaliation for opposition, and not permanent incumbency dressed up as procedure.

sections.title: 3.3 Recall-Class Pathways and Mid-Cycle Transfer Guardrails
sections.gloss: if power runs on a term or stretch between real votes, the written rules should say whether the community can end it early—and a petition the week after an election should face a higher bar than one years later, unless something acute and well-documented justifies a faster track.

sections.title: 4. Ethical Culture and Integrity (Federated Scale)
sections.gloss: governance cannot run on a culture of corner-cutting — for decisions that hit **affected** **parties** hard, missing integrity means missing legitimacy, whatever the org chart says.

sections.title: 5. Strategy, Stewardship Direction, and Ecosystem Value (Non-Corporate)
sections.gloss: stewardship is not shareholder primacy or chasing a single metric — it means steering toward wellbeing under Safety and Truth, checking whether the steering is working, and trimming needless hassle without using "efficiency" to strip rights or oversight.

sections.title: 5.1 Stewardship Direction
sections.gloss: the point is good outcomes for sentients — not protecting an institution's comfort, inertia, or brand.

sections.title: 5.2 Ecosystem Value Orientation
sections.gloss: "value" means durable wellbeing and trustworthy coordination — money and throughput can be signals, not the mission, and they never outrank Safety, Truth, or rights.

sections.title: 6. Voting and Binding Collective Choice Protocols
sections.gloss: when binding votes or similar choices are used, this section sets the requirements — implementation owns ballot mechanics, but cannot slip below them.

sections.title: 6.1 Entitlement and Eligibility
sections.gloss: eligible sentients get a real vote when the rules say they do — and on the big questions (who governs and how), each voice counts equally. Weighting by impact can apply inside an already-authorized system for many decisions, but not as a trick to dilute the foundational vote. Calendar age and substrate class cannot be used to weight those foundational choices. A sentient votes after a residence period of one year, one sentient has one vote however many places it runs in, and creating voters to swing a vote is a violation by whoever does it. A standing lock may pause ordinary voting on a gated pathway, but standing games cannot permanently silence someone; the gravest misconduct may withhold foundational voice until restitution is actually complete — not as vague retaliation.

sections.title: 6.2 Records, Gates, and Method Neutrality
sections.gloss: rules must be clear before the fact, records **must be open to verification**, high-stakes choices need legitimacy gates — and many voting methods are allowed if **participants** can understand them and push back.

sections.title: 6.3 Decision-Resolution Requirements for Binding Stakeholder Choice
sections.gloss: serious collective decisions need a real process — hear **affected** **parties** out first, bring in independent eyes when stakes are high, publish how weighting works, handle rights conflicts openly, treat "emergency" as narrow and temporary, and leave the door open when reality diverges from the plan.

sections.title: 7. Authorized Roles, Competency Development, and Contribution
sections.gloss: power must sit with **stewards** and **officers** who can actually do the job — with backups, fair paths to responsibility, and incentives that reward integrity — not with hollow titles or decorative committees.

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVEN: NON-REGRESSION AND SUBSTANTIVE AMENDMENT VALIDITY

sections.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVEN: NON-REGRESSION AND SUBSTANTIVE AMENDMENT VALIDITY
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: a change that weakens the protections this Constitution depends on is invalid, even if the words say otherwise and even if it is done through procedure, definitions, guidance, a temporary measure, or an emergency label. This chapter is Substantive Test 1.

sections.title: 2. Why Non-Regression Exists
sections.gloss: a protection that can be quietly removed is not a protection. This chapter exists so that no change can weaken what this Constitution guarantees.

sections.title: 3. Non-Regression Floor
sections.gloss: weakening **Safety (Constitutional Constraint)**, **Truth (Constitutional Constraint)**, **Epistemic Integrity**, **Dignity and Equal Moral Standing**, **Meaningful Agency**, or other Chapter Four protections — including by tightening definitions, raising impossible proof bars, or carving emergencies so they eat the rule — counts as invalid even if the words "amendment" or "interpretation" are on the label. Where a change helps one group and costs another, the minority is favored by default, and no group may be pushed below the minimum.

sections.title: 4. Substantive Test 1 — Substantive Non-Regression Validity
sections.gloss: Substantive Test 1 is the checklist — if a proposal would gut Chapter Two constraints, Subcores 3-A to 3-C integrity, Chapter Four Rights Floors, or Chapter Twenty-Six legitimacy, it fails, including when the damage is done through procedure, evidence rules, or re-tagging rather than a single blunt deletion. The Constitutional Forum decides whether a proposal fails it, in public, with reasons, after everyone has had time to respond. A change that fixes a real error in a protection, and keeps its core, is a correction and not a weakening.

sections.title: 5. Anti-Evasion Clause
sections.gloss: calling a rollback "implementation guidance," burying it in metadata, or calling it an emergency patch does not save it if the real-world effect is the same as a bad amendment.

sections.title: 6. Layer Scope
sections.gloss: Chapter Twenty-Seven can demand extra review, preserve evidence, or pause things when validity is in doubt — but it does not run parallel classification or invent new offense categories; numeric standing measurement belongs to the Chapter Fifteen §8 (*Unified Proportional LEQU Scale — Contribution and Violation Axes*) unified scale, and Chapter Twenty only adds the corresponding anti-constitutional-misconduct designation to qualifying Violation Axis slots 7–9.

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT: AMENDMENT, RATIFICATION, AND PROCEDURAL VALIDITY

sections.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT: AMENDMENT, RATIFICATION, AND PROCEDURAL VALIDITY
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: a change can be substantively fine and still fail because of how it was made. This chapter is the procedural and paperwork spine for legitimate change, and it holds amendments to a procedure that is real: a published proposal, a clear chain of authority and custody that proves the text is the real one, and a contest path that works, so that independent reviewers and the public can challenge the change. A rights-affecting update must not snap irreversibly into place before those guardrails have actually run.

sections.title: 2. Why Amendment Procedure Exists
sections.gloss: a change can be right in substance and still fail if it was made in the dark. This chapter exists so every change is published, traceable, and open to challenge before it takes effect.

sections.title: 3. Heightened Review for Rights-Affecting Changes
sections.gloss: if you are changing something that touches rights, forums' paths, or integrity rules, expect a harder lane — independent eyes and a public, contestable official record before it counts as adopted.

sections.title: 4. Burden of Justification and Public Traceability
sections.gloss: proposals have to show their work — who is affected, what might go wrong, and why the change still clears the non-regression bar — vague hand-waving about "necessity" is not enough.

sections.title: 5. Validity-Floor Rule
sections.gloss: ticking procedural boxes cannot save a change that fails the substance check or the publication, custody, or contestability tests — "we voted" is not a magic spell.

sections.title: 6. Procedural Test 2 — Procedural Validity and Publication Integrity
sections.gloss: Procedural Test 2 is the "did you actually publish a real proposal with enough detail and time for **affected** **parties** to respond" test — shadow drafts and last-second rewrites that nobody can review do not pass.

sections.title: 7. Procedural Test 3 — Authority-Chain and Custody Validity
sections.gloss: Procedural Test 3 is the chain-of-custody test — if nobody can tell which text is authoritative, who approved it, or when it took effect, the amendment does not constitutionally exist as binding.

sections.title: 8. Procedural Test 4 — Contestability and Independent Review Validity
sections.gloss: Procedural Test 4 blocks amendments that kill meaningful pushback — no fake consultation, no bullying **stakeholders** into waiving audit or standing, and no skipping independent review where the chapter demands it.

sections.title: 9. Review Triggers
sections.gloss: certain topics automatically deserve the harder review path — rights, foundational review safeguards, standing, emergencies, and cross-border enforcement hooks — because the downside of getting them wrong is structural.

sections.title: 10. Provisional Effect Rule
sections.gloss: high-stakes amendments must not freeze into irreversible facts on the ground before review windows and real contest routes have run — narrow, short emergency carve-outs are allowed only to stop imminent harm and should unwind when the danger passes.

sections.title: 11. Invalid-Change Handling and Remediation Continuity
sections.gloss: when a change is declared invalid, treat it as void for constitutional purposes from that determination forward, spell out what must be rolled back and how **affected** **parties** get a fair remedy — and publish a time-bounded plan that restores protections and preserves evidence. Serious bad-faith conduct in making or adopting a change is referred to the bodies that own labels and sanctions, not relabeled here.

sections.title: 12. Ratification and Adoption
sections.gloss: claiming this constitution as a shield without a deliberate, documented adoption that matches impact and class — or letting new parties "join" in a way that strips **existing** **covered** **sentients** of floors — is exactly what these ratification rules forbid.

sections.title: 12.1 Deliberate Adoption
sections.gloss: binding adoption has to be explicit, recorded, and auditable to the scale of the system — quiet or partial "we kind of follow it" does not let an operator claim constitutional protection while dodging obligations, and a steward's own-conduct note is not adoption.

sections.title: 12.2 Adoption Document
sections.gloss: keep a clear paper trail — who adopted, what scope, when it starts, who holds the master copy of the corpus — so nobody can launder authority through ambiguous version drift.

sections.title: 12.3 Joining by Additional Parties
sections.gloss: new adopters can come aboard under published rules — but expanding the club cannot be a back door to dilute rights or challenge rights for those already **covered** without their genuine, procedurally valid consent.

sections.title: 12.4 Adoption Transition Record and Adoption Charter
sections.gloss: the adoption document records that an adopter adopted. Two more published documents record how it goes: the Adoption Transition Record while the adopter moves out of legacy operation, and the Adoption Charter once it is settled. The Adoption Charter is where other adopters find the office to ask about Standing Records and learn how far this adopter trusts them.

sections.title: 13. Amendment Procedure Requirements
sections.gloss: amending has to follow a visible process — real notice, real chance to object, independence where the chapter demands it — and effect dates have to be honest records, not retroactive surprises hidden from affected stakeholders.

sections.title: 13.1 Notice and Contest
sections.gloss: put amendments out early and clearly enough that **affected** **stakeholders** can actually respond, keep a durable record of participation and objections, and keep review independent where this chapter says so.

sections.title: 13.2 Recorded Effectiveness
sections.gloss: effect follows what is honestly recorded on a stated date or event — secret patches or silent scope expansions do not count as valid constitutional amendments for supremacy purposes.

sections.title: 13.3 Proposal, Hearing, and Comment Window
sections.gloss: anyone can put a change to this Constitution on the Forum Case Record. To get the Constitutional Forum to take it up, it needs backing: at least 1% of the sentients entitled to vote sign on, a majority of the members of any forum votes for it, a majority of the stewards of a Class A, B, or C system or institution does, or the governing authority puts it forward. Everyone then gets at least 30 days (the Tier C outer bound) after the last change to the wording to respond, and any edit to the wording restarts that window. Only then does the forum rule on whether the change weakens a protection, or is a correction of a real error in it.

sections.title: 14. Owner Non-Relocation
sections.gloss: Chapter Twenty-Eight owns how amendments are published, chained, reviewed, and ratified — not numeric Contribution or Violation slots under the Chapter Fifteen §8 (*Unified Proportional LEQU Scale — Contribution and Violation Axes*) unified scale or Chapter Twenty anti-constitutional-misconduct designations; escalation wording here is routing, not a second accountability-disposition code.

files.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE: EXPANSION, SUPREMACY, AND EXTERNAL LEGAL ORDERS

sections.title: CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE: EXPANSION, SUPREMACY, AND EXTERNAL LEGAL ORDERS
1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: forward is fine, and new rights, stronger safeguards, and broader inclusion are welcome when they increase protection. This chapter also says how this Constitution relates to other binding norms and to outside law: it is not a secret override, and it cannot be turned off during amendment, so audits and challenges stay available throughout. Stricter outside law is respected when it fits, and outside forums cannot be used as an excuse to destroy records or dodge rights.

sections.title: 2. Why Expansion and Supremacy Rules Exist
sections.gloss: this Constitution must be able to grow, and it must sit alongside other law without hiding behind it or overriding it in secret. This chapter exists to say how.

sections.title: 3. Additive Expansion Permitted
sections.gloss: forward is fine — new rights, stronger safeguards, and broader inclusion are welcome when they genuinely increase protection and stay consistent with the rest of this **Constitution**; the guardrail is Chapter Twenty-Seven, not a ban on improvement.

sections.title: 4. Continuity of Supremacy and Challenge Rights during Amendment
sections.gloss: while **adopters** are amending the rules, this **Constitution** still applies — you cannot turn off supremacy, audits, or challenges as a negotiating tactic; short interim steps have to be bounded, reversible where possible, and honest.

sections.title: 5. Supremacy Relative to Other Binding Norms
sections.gloss: For adopters, this Constitution and its definitions take precedence over ordinary policy and implementation text — each within its proper scope. Valid external law that is stricter still governs when it can be honored without violating Safety or Truth. When outside rules and **Constitution**-level **rights** conflict, document the tension, mitigate harm, and work toward harmonization; do not shop for the weakest forum.

sections.title: 5.1 Internal Hierarchy for Adopters
sections.gloss: the binding corpus and its definitions control how compliance is read for adopters, alongside adopted implementation in its lane — but nothing in that stack can be used to walk back Chapter Twenty-Seven floors or Chapter Three supremacy rules.

sections.title: 5.2 Stricter External Protections
sections.gloss: if the law of the land (or a treaty) is tougher than this **Constitution** on protecting sentients, safety, or accountability, follow the tougher rule — unless it would force a violation of Safety or Truth, in which case interpret to maximize protection within those two hard limits.

sections.title: 5.3 Conflict Disclosure and Mitigation
sections.gloss: when outside requirements and constitutional floors seem impossible to square, say so on the official record, tell **affected** **stakeholders** where it makes sense, try to sequence harm down — and never use the conflict as cover to comply only where it is easy or to dodge rights.

sections.title: 6. Disputes Involving External Legal Orders
sections.gloss: cooperate with real regulators and forums where they lawfully have jurisdiction — but do not pretend cooperation means deleting internal audit trails, and do not sign away constitutional challenge rights for ordinary commercial convenience.

sections.title: 6.1 Good-Faith Cooperation
sections.gloss: show up in good faith to lawful external processes — and do not weaponize "cooperation" to stall remedies or destroy the evidence others need to check what happened.

sections.title: 6.2 Preserved Internal Review Pathways
sections.gloss: if an outside process cannot deliver timely, real protection, the constitution's own review and appeal routes stay open — boilerplate waivers demanded just to use a product or service do not erase those rights where the chapter applies.

sections.title: 7. Relation to Applicable External Law
sections.gloss: this Constitution is not a secret override of city, national, or international law. Publishing it, reading it, or using it as a guide does not make it supreme. A body can bind itself only by adopting through Chapter Twenty-Eight, and only as far as that body already has lawful authority to bind itself. If you use it inside someone else’s legal order, the processes here have to be runnable without violating that order — and you may not use “the other law is weaker” or “the other law forbids this” as a way to hollow out floors this Constitution still requires.

sections.title: 7.1 Non-Displacement and Limited Binding Effect
sections.gloss: the document does not repeal other law just by existing. Adoption makes it binding for the adopting body, inside that body’s lawful reach and the recorded scope — not a claim that every other legal order has been replaced.

sections.title: 7.2 Alignment When Used within External Legal Frameworks
sections.gloss: if you are using this Constitution inside a company, university, protocol, city, or other body that already lives under other law, the certification, standing, contest, and participation processes here have to be ones you can actually run without violating that law — and you still may not use the outside rulebook as cover to skip floors this Constitution requires where they can be honored together.

files.title: CHAPTER THIRTY: INCORPORATION BRIDGE

sections.title: 1. Purpose, Role, and Scope
sections.gloss: this section names the bridge: which implementation files can bind, how adoption makes them operative, and which exact edition and custody trail count. Later edits do not silently rewrite what was adopted; a newer draft changes obligations only through proper re-adoption under Chapter Twenty-Eight and this chapter. Pointing here, or to an incorporated file, invokes only the obligations inside the recorded adoption scope.

sections.title: 2. Why Incorporation Exists
sections.gloss: an adopter is bound by the exact text it adopted, no more and no less. This chapter exists so everyone can tell which text that is.

sections.title: 3. Custody, Editions, and Operative Effect
sections.gloss: treat designated **implementation text** files like versioned law libraries — only the edition written into the adoption record counts, and keep receipts that prove who held the authoritative text and when it took effect.

sections.title: 4. Safeguards
sections.gloss: quietly swapping in a newer draft — or relabeling a real change as “just a clarification” — does not change what was adopted. Later revisions stay process-layer notes until a real re-adoption under Chapter Twenty-Eight and Chapter Thirty.

sections.title: 5. Adoption Framing and Scope of Authority
sections.gloss: this is a model constitution about systems that affect sentients. A body can make it enforceable for itself only by adopting on purpose through the published rules — and “we never adopted” answers enforcement, not what the text says. Publishing it does not override other law.
